  • the Geneva stripes: their profile is the photograph's light; the faces the photographs don't show (the plates' inner faces) take the same;
  • the dial: its screws' and pin's sizes the German dial's; the serial's two strokes under the seconds hand (the 4's upright below its crossbar, the 7's bar 0.4 under the head), drawn straight on from what shows;
  • the bowl: its foot below 8.3 under the cone (unseen, run to the drawn floor), its inside (the bore and a cone 3.4 inside the outer one), the rim's top flush with the flange and its notch for the ring's pin, the thread not drawn; the brackets' plates' and web's thicknesses, the block's depth taken 4.6 with its outer face at the drawings' r 66.5 for the ring's pivot screw, the locking bracket's crank; the closing plate's spring and screw's head height;
  • the bezel's inside and its glass: the glass 4.0 thick, standing 2.5 proud, its underside 0.65 over the minute hand's boss; the seat, sight bore and shoulder not seen; the knurl drawn straight, not diamond;
  • the boxes: the walls, the glazed lid's glass and frame, the hinges, the lids opening together; the outer box's height, parting line, walls, felt and straps (its width, notch and catch measured: X5); the lid's tab drawn filling the notch;
  • the physics: the 6MX's own escapement, from its bodies weighed on the page's solids (X5); its mainspring the drawings'; the gimbals' periods the drawings' (its bowl, hanging 13.2 lower, isn't weighed apart: Unresolved);
  • the electrical contact: the lever, staff, stone, cock and spiral's places from Romanov's Fig. 100 mapped onto the photographed parts (±1.5), the base's inner edge (±2), the blocks' outlines, the contact wheel's tooth depth and form, the springs' sizes (±15 %), the jewels' sizes and the staff's pivots (each 0.02 off its cap jewel, 0.04 endshake: no photograph shows them inside their settings; the upper ended 0.1 into its stone until 24 October 2026), every screw's thread; which half-second the contact is open; the stud's outer face kept at r 44.0 and the stone's bevel to 0.3, so the lever swings clear.
Left out, small: 1
  • Left out, small: the stud's Ø 0.8 round at its point; the balance rim's graduation (05 03 01-1: "8 Körner in 60 Teilung"). The barrel bridge's pin holes' 0.3 × 90° countersinks, the upper cock's pins' 0.2 × 90° sinks (16 October 2026) and the dust bush's bottom, a flat ring 0.5 wide with the face dished 5° to the bore (26 October 2026; a 5° × 0.5 chamfer until then) are in; the dust plate's 0.5 × 45° (05 06 00-1, on the face toward the plates) and the cover plate's outer 45° (05 06 00-4, on its outer face with the sinks; not sized, scaled on the section 0.6-0.7 and drawn 0.65, leaving a 0.15 land: estimated) since 25 October 2026 (fusee.js, chamf).

3. The escapement

The Wempe's spring detent escapement is laid out on one sheet, 05 04_1 (Hemmung für Feder-Chronometer, 10:1): the escape wheel 10.00 mm from the balance, the locking stone 36.5° on from the line of centres, the impulse 21° either side of it. Its parts come from their own sheets: the escape wheel's tooth (05 04_23), the detent and its gold passing spring (1436, 05 04 01-2), the rollers and the balance.

3.1 Solved from the layout (makeEsc)

Method. The shared escapement solver, makeEsc, takes the layout's points put in its frame, the parts' shapes and bodies (the balance weighed on the model's solids, the train behind the escape wheel, the detent about its flexure), and solves the escapement as the Hamilton's is solved: the wheel released from rest chasing the impulse stone, the strike's loss, the unlocking's work, the detent's fall and ride on the tooth it has just let go; then the swing at which the escapement's work each oscillation balances the balance's damping, at the drive 05 06_20's measured force gives through the train. The rate is Airy's sum of the escapement's disturbances with the drawn hairspring's own isochronism (section 8).

3.2 In time (dynamics.js)

Method. The balance, the escape wheel with the whole train behind it, and the detent move as bodies through every contact, beat by beat, on contact geometry worked out apart from makeEsc's: the bevelled discharge stone on the gold spring's square end by separating axes, the stone on the tooth it let go from the tooth's drawn arcs. The result is held against makeEsc's: the swing, where the tooth lands, the detent's fall and its home, the rate and its isochronism. Then the detent's estimates are varied, the chronometer is started by a twist, starved of drive, knocked, and taken to sea.

3.3 The detent as a frame (tripping.js)

Method. The detent becomes a plane frame: beam elements with stretching, bending and their consistent mass for the spring (0.07 × 1.9 mm, clamped at its foot), the blade's two sections, the horn and the gold spring along its drawn path; the square with the gold spring's head and the pipe with the stone rigid. Its modes carry it in time with the balance and the wheel through elastic contacts: the discharge stone on the gold spring, the gold spring on the horn, the pipe on its banking (the block's cross screw), the tooth on the stone and on the impulse stone. Validated rigid against dynamics.js, it is then run as drawn, with its estimates varied, pushed to larger swings, and knocked.

4. The mainspring and the fusee

The drawing set has a sheet no other chronometer's drawings are known to have: 05 06_20 (Herb. Müller, 24.7.41), the fusee's curve and its measured force, the pull in grams on a lever 262 mm long over the whole wind. It gives the strip (15 × 0.37) but not its length or free shape.

Method. The Hamilton's mainspring.py solves the strip in the drawn barrel (Ø 38.5 on the arbor's Ø 13.3 core) for its shape of least bending energy at every quarter turn, coils pressing on each other, its torque the energy's slope. Its free curve is the Hamilton's measured one scaled to the length, its turns scaled by a set. Set up ¾ turn (the sheet's "3/4 Umgang gespannt") and wound through the drawn fusee and chain, its torque on the fusee arbor at each of the sheet's readings is set against the measured force, each scaled to its mean. Twelve lengths and sets were solved; the best fit is the model's spring.

The level is the drawing's open figure.

5. The energy budget

Method. Where the drive goes, from the mainspring through the fusee and chain, the train and the escapement to the balance's damping, each loss from the Wempe's own parts: the coils' friction (section 4), the barrel on its journals, the chain's links on their rivets, the fusee arbor's pivots; each mesh tooth by tooth (section 6) and each pivot on its tooth loads; the escapement's strike and unlocking (makeEsc). The balance's damping, which no Wempe source gives, is built from its parts: the air's drag on its masses, timing weights, screws and arm (a pressure drag at the masses' Reynolds number), the endstone's friction under the balance's weight, the spring's own. Then: does some balance within its parts' damping swing the sources' band on the measured drive?

6. The going train, tooth by tooth

Method. The train is four meshes: the fusee wheel (90) on the centre pinion (14), centre wheel 90 on the intermediate pinion 12, intermediate 80 on the seconds pinion 10, seconds 80 on the escape pinion 10; every count, module, tip and root from the wheels' tables, the two pinions no sheet gives fixed by the drawn centres. gearing.js takes the page's own outlines, places each pair at its drawn holes, and for 120 steps through a pitch turns the pinion back against its load until the outlines touch, giving the torque it receives with the teeth's friction (µ 0.10-0.20, steel leaves on brass). The four ratios as their wheels turn drive the balance through the escapement's equation over six hours. Then each mesh's centres are moved until it jams or its friction takes the swing out of the model's band: the window the holes must hold.

7. The parts' strength

Method. Fully wound, at the measured level of the drive, every stage lossless (the largest forces): the mainspring's bending stress; the chain's plates, rivets and hooks under its pull; the band; each mesh's teeth by Lewis' formula (Y 0.2, clock teeth); the pivots as cantilevers carrying their arbor's whole load; the maintaining spring, ratchet and click wheel; a strong hand on the key against the stop. Each against its material's published range: the margin at its weak and its strong end (~~ where only the strong end holds).

The maintaining spring. Its eye's pin goes up into the ratchet and its other pin down into the fusee wheel (05 06_4's Schnitt A-B: the eye's pin drawn whole, "Stift nach oben", the other hidden), so the drive closes the open ring until its ends nearly meet, its outer edge leaving the wheel's recess; the end at the wheel's pin, its short wide tail against the recess's wall, is held as clamped. Its stiffness from its drawn section (the width traced round it on 05 06 01-1), by Castigliano at small turns and as an elastica as it closes; how far the fusee's drive (05 06_20) closes it and where its ends would meet; its stress; and, the key held, the train run on it, the swing following, with the maintaining detent catching the ratchet up to a tooth late. wempe_sustaining.js.

8. The hairspring and Phillips' curves

The hairspring is a helix (05 03_6: 0.285 × 0.52, Ø 12.8, left-hand), its ends bent to a curve drawn on 05 03_7 as a table of radii every 10°, and cut, before the curves are bent, "auf 13 Umgänge −3,5 mm": to 13 turns less 3.5 mm.

Method. The length is read four ways and each gives the balance a period. The curve's table is fitted as two compass arcs and tested against Phillips' conditions (1861): its centroid on the perpendicular to the junction's radius, at R²/l from the staff, so that the spring pulls the balance with a pure couple. The force it leaves on the pivots under a couple follows (HSPR.lateral), with the helix's turns varied. At large swings the drawn spring is solved as an inextensible elastica by shooting and again as co-rotational beam elements; the two must agree on the couple's shape, the force and the rate.

9. Temperature: the cut bimetallic balance

A steel hairspring weakens as it warms, so the balance must open to compensate: the rim, steel inside and brass outside, cut beside the arm, curls in as it warms and carries its four masses toward the staff. How much depends on where the masses sit on the free arc.

Method. Each quarter of the rim is a bimetal cantilever from the arm's edge to the cut, curling by Timoshenko's bimetal (1925), each element's radius moving by the layers' mean growth, the masses clamping the rim over their slot. Every part is weighed on the model's solids. The spring's own loss is its thermoelastic coefficient's (−240 to −270 × 10⁻⁶) with its expansion. The rim's "Nickelstahl Sonderlegierung" is read as Guillaume's 42-44 % nickel steel (estimated); a plain nickel steel is tried beside it. The secondary error (Dent's, 2 s) against Guillaume's nickel steel as NBS Circular 58 tabulates it, checked against the 6MX passports' S.

The frame, train and escapement in heat and cold

The plates, pillars, bridges, wheels and, unlike the Hamilton's, the escape wheel (05 04 05-1, Ms 63) are brass; the pinions, arbors and detent steel, the gold spring gold, the impulse roller beryllium copper. Over the TU's working range, 4 to 36 °C, assembled at 20 °C, what isn't brass moves against what is.

Method. Each mesh's depth changes by the pinion's pitch radius times the brass's and steel's difference, against gearing_wempe.json's windows; each arbor's endshake by its brass gap and steel length (the bench's stacks, wempe_endshake.js), against the 1958 MX repair book's bands. The escapement runs through makeEsc in the brass wheel's own frame: the steel detent from its brass-held foot (the depth of lock, the gold spring's tip), the rollers on the steel staff, the springs' moduli and the mainspring's torque by their thermoelastic coefficients; at the published constants' middle and at the corner that moves each part most (brass 20.9, steel 10.8 × 10⁻⁶ a °C), with the drawn lock and with the bench's, the window's middle. Where makeEsc loses the impulse, dynamics.js --model wempe in time was run on the same settings and agrees (the swing 91-97°, the detent leaving the discharge stone 4.9° early).

Found. The depths, endshakes, lock and chain hardly notice (under 4 µm). The gold spring's tip does: 1.8-2.3 µm farther from the staff at 36 °C, taking 0.3-0.45° of the 1.50° let-off, and the escapement loses its impulse at about 1.0-1.1° (the same edge that tops wempe_tolerances.js's lock window). The lock window that holds over the range is about half the one at 20 °C, and since 3.45.00 it is the window wempe_tolerances.js gives the bench (the owner's choice): 231.7-237.9 µm, the bench aiming just under its top (237.8) so the teeth's wear, which only makes the lock shallower, has three years' room. At the constants' corner no lock holds at 36 °C (open).

10. The case and gimbals

Method. The bowl with the movement in it and the gimbal ring are weighed on the model, every closed solid at its material's density (massprops.py --model wempe): mass, centre of gravity and inertia about the gimbal centre. 05 01 says to move the case brackets "bis Gleichgewicht erreicht ist", until it hangs level, and the tool does so. The two bodies then run on their pivots under the Hamilton's seaway (gimbals.js: narrow-band random roll, pitch, yaw and heave; NORDFORSK's 0.12 g limit), and what reaches the balance's staff is run through the Wempe's escapement.

11. The 6MX's trial and a voyage

The Soviet copy of the Einheits-Chronometer, the 6MX, was made to a published specification (TU 25-07.1533-84) with a trial: 35 days at 36, 20, 4, 20 and 36 °C, the first two days of each period not counted, wound daily, its figures worked as E (the mean variation of the daily rate), R, D, C (the temperature coefficient), S (the secondary error), each period's mean, and N = 42E + 4.5R + 60C + 2.4S. No Wempe test card is to hand, so the trial is the 6MX's.

Method. Each day's rate is summed from its parts: the temperature curve (section 9, with the masses set by the adjuster at their compensating place to ±0.25°), the air's density, the swing over the daily wind, the day-to-day scatter and drift (calibrated on eight 6MX test cards' E and R), the barometer and the oil; the trial is drawn 2,000 times. Then a 60-day voyage from a winter port into the tropics, rated over ten days in port, gives the error a navigator would carry.

12. Building it: tolerances, the bench, the Monte Carlo

The checks above take the Wempe as drawn. A chronometer made to the drawings is made to tolerances, some the sheets give and some they don't, and is then tested and adjusted on the bench as its makers did. Three tools follow it there, as the Hamilton's tolerances.js, bench.js and montecarlo.js do. They are guidance for anyone who would make one, proved by their own runs: the model was never made.

12.1 How closely the unsized parts must be made

Method. From the escapement as the page runs it (makeEsc with the Wempe's settings, driven by 05 06_20's force through the train), the swing and rate are solved with the escape wheel's torque and the detent's and gold spring's stiffness each scaled (a strip's stiffness as its thickness cubed). Each part's range is the one that keeps the swing in the model's guard band, 193-270°, over the whole 56-hour wind; the sources' 225-270° is reported beside it. The parts: the mainspring's strip (05 06_20's "15 × 0,37", no tolerance), the detent's spring (1436's faint "0,07") and its preload, the gold spring, the depth of lock (05 04_1's 0.175, set by the banking), and the hairspring against the period, which the timing weights must take up.

12.2 The tests on the bench

Method. Each test turns the model's figures into what a made part or movement must read, and how to measure it with a maker's means: the mainspring's pull against 05 06_20, the fusee's evenness, the depths, the endshake from the sheets' fits, the balance vibrated, its free run-down, the detent's ring, the escapement's figures and the banking's preload, the swing, the maintaining spring, and the 6MX TU's 35-day trial as the acceptance test (the Wempe's sheets give no trial of their own).

12.3 The whole movement made to tolerances

Method. 2,000 movements, each drawing every tolerance at once (uniform within the sheets' limits where they give them, normal where estimated): the arbors' holes, every term of each arbor's endshake stack from its sheet, the mainspring's strip, the teeth's friction, the detent's and gold spring's strips, the wheel's tips and the banking (the depth of lock), the preload, the hairspring's strip, coil, cut length and modulus. Each is judged as made (the train turns, every arbor free, the escapement unlocks and locks in its window, the swing in the guard band over the wind, it times within the weights' reach), then after the bench's tests as a maker applies them (bench_wempe.json's figures): a close mesh re-bushed, endshake set again, a detent spring out of its band replaced, the banking and preload set, another strip, the set-up turned, the hairspring matched to the balance.

13. The whole transmission in time

Sections 3 to 7 take the movement a mechanism at a time, each with the others held still or rigid. Here every part that moves is one system: the barrel on its solved mainspring, the chain, the fusee with its two clicks, the maintaining ratchet, spring and detent, the fusee wheel and the going train to the escape wheel, the motion work and hands, the up-and-down work, the key and the stop: each a body with its inertia weighed on the model's solids (or estimated, said where), joined by the elements a real movement has, none of them linearised.

Method. wempe_transmission.js. The elements: the mainspring's torque as solved (section 4) with its coils' friction as a stick-slip element, so winding takes more than running gives; the chain in tension only, so it can go slack, its lever on the fusee where it lies and rising and falling as each 2.05 mm link comes onto a drum; each pawl (the clicks, the maintaining detent) a body on its pivot under its spring, riding the teeth's backs and catching a face only if it is down; the maintaining spring's drawn ring, stiffening as it closes, with its bank; every mesh tooth by tooth on the page's own outlines (section 6's), the driven gear's place under load through each pitch, the backlash to its back flank and the teeth's friction, contact on either flank or neither; the cannon pinion's friction fit, which slips past its torque; the key's one-way coil spring (it grips whenever the hand holds the key against the fusee, and slips only if the key is turned the wrong way); the stop bar on its pin. The escapement is dynamics.js's own (section 3.2), its escape wheel driven each step by the train through the escape pinion's mesh, at its own place and speed. The beat runs from 8 starts of the train's meshes, and each mesh's peak is judged on the worst of them, a figure that holds as the step is refined (wempe_transmission_converge.js: the seconds wheel's, the escape pinion's take-up after the escape wheel lands on its stone, within 2 % from a quarter of the step to an eighth). It is stepped in time at a microsecond. The stiffnesses no sheet gives (the teeth's give, the chain's, the clicks' faces, the bank) are estimated from the parts, and those the results rest on are varied.

Watch the run: the movement in plan, every part coloured by the load it carries against its running load and its deviations from rigid motion magnified, as a finite-element post-processor shows a deformed shape; a beat, the key let go outright and eased back, and the stop, played in slow motion with their time histories (wempe_transmission_trace.js).

Every moving part in 3D

The runs above give the forces between the parts; here each moving part's own stress under them. motion3d.py takes the page's solids and moves each part as the page's own update() moves it; motion3d_fe.py solves each part as finite elements (voxel bricks on its solid, a modulus by its material, finer windows at its contacts, the root's bending kept apart from the contact's pressure) at its worst load in the four runs, held where it is held; the springs (the mainspring by its solved curvature, the hairspring, the maintaining spring, the gold spring) from their large-deflection solutions. Each part is read against its drawn material: the 1950s build beside the drawing's.

Open the 3D viewer: every moving part in 3D through the four runs, coloured by its stress, its stress against its material's limit or its speed, the deviations magnified, with each part's load, margin and motion, the kinematics against the tooth counts, and the assumptions.

Every part past its limit but the mainspring (its inner coils, fully wound: section 17's builds and wempe_build.js take it up) is past it only with the key let go outright. Those peaks lie at the contacts, and the methodology's contact study finds them the contact's own pressure: it halves as the load is spread twice as wide, so a real blow dents the click's nose and the tooth's face where they meet. By the beam formulas only the maintaining ratchet's teeth bend past brass (about 500 MPa at the blow); the click wheel's tooth carries about 200 MPa in the contact study (240-280 until 26 October 2026), inside it. The let-go study (wempe_letgo_fix.js) runs that let-go (the worst place, the nearer click 97 % of the way to the next; and eased back beside it) with the fixes a maker could make: more clicks, evenly spaced over a tooth, so the fusee runs a shorter way free; a brake, friction between the click wheel and the maintaining ratchet, which the clicks hold still running (so it costs the train nothing) but which the key works against winding; the click's face cushioned. The stresses are the 3D results' scaled to each case's force; the click wheel's tooth by wempe_strength.js's beam, the highest of three readings (the FE on the tooth gives 0.49 MPa a newton (0.60 until 26 October 2026), wempe_ratchets.js 1.16, the beam 2.05: the methodology's cross-checks).

14. Against a period text

The drawings decide the Wempe; a period text says how a detent escapement was usually proportioned, and so where the Wempe's makers chose otherwise. keystone.js --model wempe measures the escapement against Watch and Clock Escapements (The Keystone, 1904), Ch. III: the wheel and roller, the balance planted where the rims cross over a pitch, the impulse and unlocking arcs, the locking stone, the tooth's face and back, the detent and its spring, the balance. The text is generic, so the tool reports and never judges; where the two differ, the drawing and its sheet are named.

15. The swing measured on video

No Wempe source gives the balance's damping, the figure the swing rests on most. A running 6MX, whose balance is of the same kind (a cut bimetallic rim, four masses, two nuts on the arm), is filmed from above at 30 frames a second in moMvyx8eXfo, 17:53-19:50 (another person's video: linked at the moment used, no frame copied here).

Method. wempe_swing.py reads the balance's arm in every frame as a drop in saturation along the rim's ellipse, folded every 180°, and fits each 4-second window with a sine: the swing, its alias settled by the frames between the turning points. The movement is set down at 17:52 and the swing rises; it is turned in the hands at 18:46 (the 6MX's start) and the swing falls back. wempe_startup.js fits all the stretches together with the Wempe's averaged balance equation, d(A²)/dt = 2 Wn(s, A)/T − 2A²·damping/TF, the escapement's work Wn from makeEsc with the Wempe's settings, the drive and each stretch's start free: rising and falling toward one swing, they fix TF, the free run-down.

The clicks of two more running chronometers were read with this escapement in time: a Lange VEB (gnIP3NqNbEU, 0:03-1:03) and a Kirova under a dome (KxInG08LWXg, 0:00-0:34). Their pairings leave the swing between readings 80-120° apart, since which click is which isn't settled, so no swing is read from them (References/wempe/VIDEOS.md, "Measured").

16. The Soviet 6MX

The page's third version (Variants, Version) is the 6MX the 1st Moscow Watch Factory made from these drawings, built as one photographed chronometer is made: Kirov No. 247 of February 1952, from Johannes Altmeppen's photographs, with videos of other 6MXs where his don't show a part. Each difference from the drawings is measured on a photograph, fitted on the sheets' hole table, or marked estimated; the drawings' two versions are left as they were (every view the same to the pixel). The section below is the model's README as it stands: how each difference was read, and how sure. The page keeps the drawings' swing and rate in every version; what the 6MX's differences would change is worked out apart (wempe_6mx.js, below).

How each difference was read (the README's "The Soviet 6MX")

Status (18 October 2026): complete. X0-X4 (16 October 2026) built the switch, the movement, the dial and finish, the case and boxes, the cards, the essay's paragraphs, the report's section and the physics worked apart; X5 (18 October 2026, below) settled what they left: every one of the 6MX gallery's photographs read for the model, the parts measured on them built (the escapement's collet and detent block, the lower cock, the ring's screws, the bowl, brackets, closing plate and outer box), its electrical contact built, and the page running the 6MX's own escapement. What no source shows stays in "Estimated" (The Soviet 6MX) and "Unresolved"; the asks for the photographs that would settle it in REQUESTS.md.

The Variants' third version, Soviet 6MX (Kirov No. 247, 1952; rev=6mx in the link): the 6MX (6МХ) the 1st Moscow Watch Factory made from these drawings after 1946-47, built as one photographed chronometer is made, as Wempe 3955 stands for the first-drawn sheets. Kirov No. 247 (February 1952, first generation) has Altmeppen's full set (photos/dg-chrono-6mx/: its dial, top plate on millimetre paper, dial side, four obliques, detent and box) and his arrowed comparisons with a Wempe. Its electrical contact (E-Kontakt) is left out. The plan is PLAN-wempe-6mx.md at the root.

X0, the switch (16 October 2026). The version control (heading "Version") has three buttons. userData.rev now lists the versions a group shows in ('last 6mx': the revised sheets' pieces the 6MX kept; 'first'; '6mx' for its own), setRev(v) shows a group if its list holds v, and each onRev callback gets the version's name. Until its own parts are built, the 6MX shows every revised piece: its views are pixel for pixel the last-revised ones (views.py --model wempe --eval "__mv.userData.setRev('6mx')"). Both earlier versions rendered unchanged, every view 0 px. The tools: audit.py --rev 6mx (its keys movement.6mx, box.6mx), ci.py's wempe-audit-6mx and wempe-exploded-6mx; bom.py's dev entries take a list of versions in rev; app.js's cards per version in REVC.

How Kirov No. 247 is measured. Its top plate (2_Kirow_247_A.jpg, square-on) is put on the sheets' hole table by a similarity on four arbors seen on it (the fusee's square in the cork ring, the barrel's square, the balance's cap jewel, the escape wheel's endstone) and pillars 11 and 49: 8.98 px/mm, every residual under 0.55 mm; holemap.py --model wempe lays it over the model's plan hole by hole (it now takes --model). Its dial side (3_Kirow_247_uZ.jpg) the same way on seven holes (the centre, seconds, change wheel, intermediate, escape and the intermediate bridge's two screws): 8.63 px/mm, under 0.42. The millimetre paper under the top plate gives the paper's scale (8.8 px/mm), not the plate's, which stands well above it. Screws' centres are circles fitted to their edges.

X1a, the frame (16 October 2026). Each piece and how sure:

  • Pillar 39 at 190° (Altmeppen's list: pillar 39 in another place). No pillar or screw at its drawn 210° on either face; its screw at 190.0° (top) and 189.6° (dial side), where 11 and 49 read 94.9/94.8° and 350.1/349.9°, their drawn bearings: sure to ±0.5°, pillar 49's 350° mirrored across the O-W line. Its radius reads 36.6-37.3 (each reading corrected by 11's and 49's in the same fit). On r 37 the drawn pillar (Ø 8.1) would stand 0.11 into the drawn seconds wheel's tips (Ø 21.9); it clears them from r 37.2, so it is drawn at r 37.3, 0.2 clear (likely; the 6MX's seconds wheel isn't seen). Both plates' holes and seats, the pillar and its two screws move with it (WD.P39_6MX).
  • No hole 20 in the upper cock (Altmeppen: no window in the upper cock; his comparison's arrow points at the Wempe's hole there). Kirov 247's cock is plain where the overlay puts it: sure.
  • No hole 53 in the top plate (Stift f. Wendelfeder, for the balance holding work): Kirov 247's plate is bare there, in plain view: likely. Holes 51 and 52 lie under its balance, unseen, and are kept.
  • Holes 3, 12 and 40 kept. Hole 3 is a clean Ø 3.6 hole at 0.3° (its Ø 3.5 at 0°), 12 at 105.0° (105°), 40 partly under the barrel bridge at 224°: so Altmeppen's "three small windows by the pillar screws" are not these Hilfslöcher, as frame.js had read them (unresolved: what he meant isn't found on Kirov 247's photographs).
  • Jewels in chatons at the intermediate arbor's two pivots and the seconds arbor's upper (Altmeppen; the TU's 15 jewels are the drawings' 12 and these three). Flush gilt settings about Ø 4.1 on both faces of Kirov 247, the pivot in the middle, no screws. Each chaton fills the bush's hole (4.59 in the plate, 4.3 in the bridge), its stone flush with the face the arbor's shoulder bears on, so the endshake stays the drawings' (likely); the stone Ø 2.2 × 0.6 and the sink estimated. bom.json's six lines carry "rev":"6mx" (a line with rev counts only in those versions), the bushes "last first", and the arbors' in relations take either (WN-300.t38|6MX.jw38u); checks.py's JEWELS is per version (15 for the 6MX).
  • The electrical contact's fixings (X5, below): the top plate's two Ø 3.5 access holes over the contact's base screws (219.0° r 37.5 and 179.1° r 38.6: the README read the 219° one, with the screw's dark slotted head 19 mm down in it, as "a cheese-head screw in the top plate at S 28.75 W 23.07"; Kirov 1564's, without the contact, are open to the pillar plate); the dial side's two flush screw ends at 180° r 38.2 and 220° r 37.9 (M1.7, open on Kirov 1564). The small hole at S 20.6 O 30.2 is on Kirov 1564's plate too: not the contact's, not built (Unresolved).

X1b, the escapement (16 October 2026). The 6MX has the escapement at the heights the sheets first drew, with the revised block's form:

  • The escape wheel just under the top plate, on a long cone collet (likely). Kirov 247's detent view (8_Kirow_247_F.jpg) and Kirov-Poljot 24020's (9_KirPol_24020_Feder2.jpg) show it so, as Wempe 3955's (10_Wempe_3955_Feder_plus.jpg, the first-drawn version's source); Altmeppen's comparison of Wempe 3955 with a 6MX (1_3_Vergleich_Wempe-6MX_Feder.jpg) marks the block, not the wheel. On 24020's, scaled by the block's base (6.5 deep, 26.6 px/mm), the wheel's teeth read 0.35-2.3 under the plate. So the 6MX takes the first-drawn balance, rollers, escape wheel and arbor and their jewels ('first 6mx'), and their Exploded offsets. The staff's form (the 1941 collar or the 1946 hub) isn't seen on any 6MX photograph: the first-drawn one, the staff the sheets draw at these heights, is built (estimated).
  • The detent at the first-drawn heights its block holds it at (the foot 1.3-3.3 under the plate), with 1436's revised (bracketed) sections (likely). It is not shorter than 1436's: the 6.4 from the pipe to the square read on the loose 6MX block until 18 October 2026 divided a foreshortened span by the scale across the block; along the detent (24.5 px/mm) it reads 8.2 (7.8-8.6), the drawn 8.4 (X5).
  • The block, 05 04 01-4 read in first angle, as the sheet itself reads (DIN's; How the balance and escapement were measured): the upright at the free face, 3.5-6.5 under the plate; on 24020's it reads 4.1-7.0, the detent's blade 2.9-4.1 above it (±0.3 with the camera): sure in kind, the sheet's figures kept. The 6MX settles, for itself, the reading the drawings leave unresolved: its block hangs its upright below the detent, at the first-drawn heights. Its foot a taper (below); the hole Ø 1.3 drilled from the plate's face to the foot's M1.
  • The banking: the cross screw through the upright, centred, its domed brass head Ø 3.4 × 1.4 (Ø 3.2 until 29 October 2026: below) on the wheel's side of the pipe, which rests on its flat face (24020's: Ø 3.2 against the upright's 3; the loose block's, 8_Gangfeder_mit_Kloben_Rus_einfach.jpg, reads Ø 3.8 by the upright's 3.0 at 26 px/mm, which would stand 0.13 into the gold spring's path as it bends aside: the mounted reading taken, likely), its thread 0.6 out behind the upright.
  • Not built: the adjusting slide. The loose block has a gilt slide in a notch across the base's plate face under a slotted cylinder, and a large slotted screw (head about Ø 3.4 on 24020's, 2.9 under the plate) in the base's end beside the detent's foot; how they meet the plate's hole 13 and which way the slide moves aren't seen (Unresolved). Nor is the collet's form: both 6MXs show one long gilt cone, about 5 long, as Wempe 3955 (Unresolved, below); the first-drawn arbor's cone and pipe are built.

X1c, the barrel (16 October 2026). The barrel cap underneath (Altmeppen's list; Knirim's, against Lange's Kal. 100): the drawings' own barrel, the 1941 three-piece barrel the first-drawn version builds (0207, 020701; its arbor's core and the mainspring 0.44 lower with it): likely. Kirov 247's side views (4_, 6_Kirow_247_N, S) show a drum about Ø 41.5 × 18 under the chain, too fine to tell that ring from the later drum turned over. The maintaining spring stays the revised one. Not built: the lower balance cock's other shape (Unresolved). Since 28 October 2026 the drawings' 1941 barrel is read with its lid on the bridge's side and its bottom on the pillar plate's (drawing check 2, 4-M1): the 6MX is built with that barrel, and which side the 6MX's own cap is on (Altmeppen's "underneath") isn't modelled apart: its discs are the same sizes either way.

X2, the dial (16 October 2026). Kirov No. 247's dial (dg-chrono-6mx/1_Kirow_247_Z.jpg), traced as the two German dials are (dialtrace.py --dial kirov, into js/dialface_kirov.js, WDIALFACE_KIROV; the Variants' dial switch, 1st Moscow Watch Factory, which choosing the 6MX selects):

  • Its layout is the drawings': the six printed circles fitted by one homography to 10-25 µm, the sub-dials' centres on the arbors at (0, ±23), measure Ø 89.96, 84.91 (the minute track's lines), 26.18 (the up-and-down circle), 37.13, 33.01 (the seconds track's), 22.79 (the seconds' inner circle), the sheet's 90, 85, 26, 37, 33, 23. Printed thin, as Lange 5177's (blur sigma 0.031 mm), its up-and-down sub-dial laid out as Lange's: the circle open at the top (338.3-22.6 deg) for СПУСК (run down) and ЗАВОД (wound) along it, the band's end strokes at 0 and 56 running in to r 5.33. Every figure of the geometric printing is dial.js's KIROV, from --dial kirov --geo.
  • Traced: the hours, the up-and-down figures 0-56, СПУСК and ЗАВОД, the seconds figures, the factory's mark 1МЧЗ and ИМЕНИ КИРОВА across the centre, and the serial 247, written in red ink: traced from red alone (red over the other channels, each stroke half way to its own core: the pen's strokes 0.40-0.45 wide, the 2's lighter), drawn #ff617f (the photograph's 165, 59, 79 on its paper's 149, 146, 145, scaled to the model's paper). Where the hands cover the printing: ИМЕНИ's last И (its lower corner under the minute hand) is its first, the same glyph; under the seconds hand's head and stem, the 4's upright (it shows at x 1.59 from its top, z 16.85, to the crossbar) is drawn on down to the line's foot (z 19.25) and the 7's bar (it shows at z 15.46 from x 3.95 to its corner) on 0.4 under the head, straight pen strokes 0.42 wide (estimated; until 16 October 2026 they were lost and the serial read 241); the brass hands' boss and their shadows are cut from the ink, not filled in.
  • Its screws at the 19, 39 and 59 minute marks (Altmeppen's list): 112.5, 233.6 and 353.1 deg on the photograph (±1 for its tilt), drawn at 114, 234 and 354, the German dial's 120 and 240 moved; the movement ring's tapped holes for them move with them (both built per version).

X2, the finish (16 October 2026). Geneva stripes on the plates, cocks and bridges (Kirov 247's, 1952; the Wempe's are hammered, drawn plain gilt): straight, 3.95 mm apart (an FFT on plain patches of its top plate, 3.73-4.28 at 8.98 px/mm, and its dial side, 3.71-4.35 at 8.63: the median), running at 50 deg in each face's own photograph (49.8-50.3 and 48.5-52.1): in plan along (-0.643, 0.766) over the top plate, cocks and barrel bridge as one sweep (its stripes run on across them), and along (0.643, 0.766) over the pillar plate's dial face and the intermediate bridge (each plate striped from its own face). Across a stripe the photograph's brightness, folded on the pitch over two patches and averaged (each to its brightest), falls slowly from 1 to 0.61 and rises quickly back: the gilt material's map (frame.js's G6), on solidGeo's plan UVs. Likely: the profile is the photograph's light; the faces it doesn't show (the plates' inner faces) take the same. Altmeppen's "the finish changed in the late 1950s" is later than Kirov 247, which is already striped. The barrel and intermediate bridges are built per version for it, their pins with them.

X3a, the bowl and bezel (16 October 2026). The 6MX's bowl isn't R-05 01 00-1 outside: no Ø 118 flange, but a threaded rim Ø 110.5 for a knurled bezel screwed onto it (Altmeppen's "the bowl and bezel brass", and Kirow 422's knurled bezel). Inside it is the drawings' (the bore, its round, the bottom, the recess and closing plate, the winding hole's seat): the movement is the drawings' and stands in it as drawn. Each reading and how sure:

  • The rim, Ø 110.5 (sure to ±1.2): on Kirov 247's dial photograph (1_Kirow_247_Z.jpg, in its bowl with the bezel off), scaled by dialtrace.py's own fit of its printed circles (8.75 px/mm, 0.01-0.03 mm rms), 24 rays round the dial read the dial's edge at r 51.0-51.2, the movement ring's gold flange to r 53.0 (its 105.95) and the bowl's dark rim outside it to r 55.0-55.6. The rim stands a little under the dial's plane, so ±0.6 for the camera. Kirov 009, 1564, 2973, 22823, 23239 and Poljot 00127's dial photographs, all in their bowls, show the same narrow rim round the flange (by eye).
  • The outside profile (likely in shape, its heights estimated): Kirow 422's bowl turned over (dg-chrono-dec/11_Kirow_DEC_422_Gehäuse.jpg, side on), its silhouette traced every 4 rows and scaled by its band (930 px) as that Ø 110.5 (8.42 px/mm). Body r 51.8 (51.6-52.2: smaller down the photograph, which lies farther from the camera), a cone to the foot, the foot read r 37.5 and taken as the drawn 36.25 (the camera, about 0.33 m off, makes the foot about 4 % larger than the band; the cone's radii are scaled down the same way, 0.962 at the foot to 0.987 at the body), a step and round out to the band (rows 448-472), the band up to the bezel's edge. The heights come from the photograph's rows, put on the movement's frame by two ends: the foot's face at the drawn YB − 65 (the floor where the cork ring's seat needs it) and the bezel's glass 0.65 over the hands. That is 0.1322 mm a row, 6.4 % more than the photograph's own vertical scale (8.05 px/mm at its widths and a 15° view). The close camera leaves that stretch unmeasured: the view tilts from 9° at the foot to over 20° at the bezel. So, from YB: the foot −65 to −62.4, the cone to −51.3, the body to −13.2, the round to the band by −10.0, the band to the bezel's edge at +0.55.
  • The threaded rim round the flange (likely): Kirov 14917 with its bezel off (rAw2zmulpk8 0:29 and 2:52, 1080p) shows the thread running up to the gold flange round the dial, and its loose bezel threaded inside. Drawn flush with the flange's top (YB + 4.7), its counterbore r 53.05 down to the drawn seat at YB. A notch 1.8 wide at 12 o'clock takes the ring's radial pin (WN-202, its end at r 55.0), down to YB + 0.8, through the thin wall under the bezel (estimated). The thread isn't drawn.
  • The bezel (likely in shape): traced on the same photograph. Its lower edge r 56.1 swells (a bell) to the knurl's tips, r 58.3 (Ø 116.6). The knurl runs over 42 rows, 5.5 mm by the stretch; it is diamond on the photographs, drawn as 360 straight teeth 0.4 deep. Then a plain lip rounds into the top face at YB + 13.5. The glass is thick and stands proud (12_Kirow_DEC_422_Kasten_1.jpg: a green edge over a narrow brass top): Ø 107 × 4.0, its top edge chamfered 0.8, its underside YB + 12.0, 0.65 over the hands' highest point (the minute hand's boss, 17.70 in the movement's frame), its top YB + 16.0, where the drawn bezel's top is. Inside (estimated: no photograph shows it): the glass's seat 1.5 deep, the sight bore r 52.1 over the dial's edge (51.8), and the shoulder at the rim's top bearing on the flange and the rim, which holds the movement down as the drawn bezel's recess does.
  • The brackets: the drawn case brackets and locking bracket, their plates on the 6MX's narrower body (r 51.8). Kirov 14917's inner pivots (rAw2zmulpk8 0:29: the cone-pointed screw in the gimbal ring's middle, below the bowl's rim) work out about 15 mm under the dial's face (YB − 10 ± 3, the frame tilted 53° by the dial's ellipse), the drawn YB − 11.5. Kirow 422's brackets stand higher (Unresolved).
  • The winding hole's shutter: Kirov 14917's foot (rAw2zmulpk8 0:12 and 0:36, the bowl turned over) has the turning closing plate in its recess, its centre screw and its round hole away from the winding hole: the drawings' (05 01 00-2), kept. The pin in a slot on Uy8A88_j-cA (5:21-5:25) is a later Polet's, not built.

X3b, the boxes (16 October 2026). Kirov No. 247's box and outer box (dg-chrono-6mx-gallery/leben-des-6mx/13_, 14_Kirow_247_Kasten_*.jpg), built in the drawings' box's place (the gimbals, pivots and transit lock as drawn):

  • The box, 190 each way (the TU's "190x190x190", 1984: the only figure; sure for the later 6MX, likely for 1952): orange lacquered wood (Kirov 247's sampled #dc6914 to #e07c3e, drawn at 0.7 of it as the mahogany is), in three tiers, as Kirov 1564's, 2973's, 22823's and 23239's (Kirov 422's and 479's, German movements finished in Moscow, have one glazed lid). The tiers measured on Kirov 22823's box, nearly square-on (bilder-zum-6mx/10_Kirow_22823_Kasten.jpg), as parts of its height at both edges: the body 97 (0.506, 0.514), the glazed lid 68 (0.354, 0.360), the top lid 25 (0.140, 0.127): likely. Kirov 247's own front puts its parting lines 72 apart by the hasp's width.
  • Its fittings (likely, by Kirov 247's front, 14_, scaled by the hasp, 53 wide: 22823's 215 of 773 px): two hasps with knurled screws (the head Ø 11 × 5 on the lower leaf, 6.4 under the line), across both parting lines; the factory's diamond badge on the glazed lid, 38.6 × 24, its centre 37.6 under the upper line, lettered "1 МЧЗ им. Кирова"; the number plate on the body, Ø 31, 40 under the lower line, "247"; brass strips 27 × 12 round each vertical corner at the bottom, 27 under the lower line, 25 under the upper and capping the top (22823's); a ring handle on each side (22823's).
  • Estimated: the walls 10; the glass in the glazed lid's top under a frame; both lids hinged at the back, opened together (the page has one lid; WCASE's rev(v) gives the page the version's lids); the bottom 93.5 under the pivots as drawn, the pivots 2.5 longer for the wider walls, the transit lock's bracket reaching the right wall, the key's shelf with legs 65 so its front edge and the key stand where the drawings' do.
  • The outer box (estimated in size): of the same wood, felt-lined, a half-round notch in the body's front at the parting line into which a half-round tab on the lid's front closes, a turning hook on the tab over a brass catch under the notch, the number plate 247 on the lid, a leather strap on each side (Kirov 247's, 13_; Poljot 08479's, 14_Poljot_08479_Kasten_komplett.jpg). No photograph scales it: 250 each way and high round the box (felt 18 under and over, 8 at the sides, walls 12), the parting line at half, the notch r 48 (13_: 0.38 of the front's width). The red cloth bag it stands in (the TU's "чехол") isn't drawn.

X4, the 6MX's physics (16 October 2026). tools/wempe_6mx.js (with wempe_inertia.py --rev 6mx, which weighs its escapement's bodies on the page's solids in that version) works out what its differences change; the page keeps the drawings' swing and rate (the user's choice):

  • The jewels in chatons change nothing the energy budget can see: the model's sources give oiled steel in ruby and in brass the same friction (μ 0.10-0.15, physics.js), so the train's efficiency is the drawings'. They tighten the pivots' shake (the jewel holes the pivot's and 0.025, estimated; the drawn bushes 0.035 and 0.05 loose), and so loosen the holes' tolerance a CNC must hold: ±82 µm against ±77 at the centre-intermediate mesh, ±60 against ±47 at the intermediate-seconds, ±35 against ±25 at the seconds-escape (the escape jewels' own shake 0.03).
  • The first-drawn balance staff and collar (no hub screws): the balance's inertia 0.01 % less, a beat shorter by about 24 µs, 4.2 s a day fast before timing (4.4 until the bodies were weighed again for 3.06.02), which the timing weights take out as they do the drawings' balance's. The detent's inertia 2.6 % less and the escape arbor's 0.1 %: the swing (191.9-202.0° over the wind, since 16 October 2026's reading of 05 04_1's angles) and the escapement's rate against 12 h are the drawings' to 0.1° and 0.01 s a day.

X5, completing it (18 October 2026). Every photograph in the 6MX gallery (dg-chrono-6mx-gallery/, thirteen more 6MXs), Kirov 14100's parts laid out (chasy-ru-9985-kirova-14100/) and Romanov's Proektirovanie priborov vremeni (1975, Figs. 95-101 and their parts lists) read for the model, each part then measured as below (the 1950s Kirovs first, Kirov 247 before the rest; the user's choice, 17 October 2026). Each reading and how sure:

  • The escape wheel's collet: one straight cone with a square shoulder onto the arbor, no pipe: Ø 2.77 at the wheel to 1.70 at its end (1.55 since 29 October 2026: below), 5.08 long on 8_Kirow_247_F.jpg (18.3 px/mm by the wheel's Ø 14 tips and the pinion's Ø 2.97), 3.14 to 1.58 over 5.23 on Kirov-Poljot 24020's (26.4 px/mm): likely. Kirov 247's built; the first-drawn version keeps 05 04_7.1's cone and pipe.
  • The detent block's fixing: not through hole 13 but by a slotted steel stud Ø 3.4 flush in the top plate's outer face, 2.2 S of it, between two steady pins 10.0 apart (holemap.py --model wempe on 2_Kirow_247_A.jpg, six seeds, 8.993 px/mm, every residual under 0.57; 2_Kirow_009_A.jpg by hand; each corrected by hole 12's 0.4 offset; the two agree to 0.3: sure to ±0.4). In the block's frame its pins stand 1.9 nearer its end than 05 04 01-4 puts them, the stud 2.1 nearer and 0.8 across from hole 13; the block itself stays where the escapement needs it (its holes drilled otherwise: Unresolved). The plate's holes per version (WESC.HOLES.block6). The near pin, 0.55 inside the end face, goes 1.2 into the block, clear above the detent foot's pins (estimated).
  • The adjusting slide and the stop screw (on the loose block, 8_Gangfeder_mit_Kloben_Rus_einfach.jpg, 30.3 px/mm across, 24.5 along, tilted 30-36°): a gilt key 3.2 wide, flush in a notch across the corner of the base's plate face and free side, from the stud to the edge and 2.5 down the side, the stud through it; a large slotted screw in the base's free side 0.9 from its end and 3.3 deep, its head Ø 4.0-4.4 over the end face by 1.2, beside the detent's foot (every 6MX Feder photograph shows it): likely in kind. Kirov 14100's loose detent has a slotted foot, so the screw is most likely a stop for the foot's place along the block, the banking setting the lock; how the slide works isn't seen (Unresolved).
  • The block's upright: slit since 29 October 2026 (below); until then no slit (the loose block's upright, its face toward the plate, is plain to its end with the banking screw's thread straight through it: likely), and a short taper at its root, widening 0.46 over its last 0.9 (about 27°, on that photograph only: estimate), where the model drew r 2 (estimated). The banking screw's head Ø 3.2 × 1.4 was taken to fit all three readings (3.3 loose, 3.1-3.4 on 247, 3.4 on 24020; the loose block's 3.8 came from the wrong scale).
  • The lower balance cock: full depth only over its lug, the rest of the bar toward the screw and pins cut back to 3.3 deep (every 6MX side view of the detent, a stamped number on the deep part; on 8_Kirow_247_F.jpg, the full depth taken as the drawn 10: 3.3, 3.0-3.9): likely; the step 1.5 past the lug's edge so the lug and the screw's hole stand on the full depth (estimated). Its plan stays the drawings', and its step is in question (the side views fix only a line across the plan; the loose piece once taken for it is the upper cock: Unresolved).
  • The movement ring's screws: at 342.2°, 102.2° and 246.4° ±0.5 (both of Kirov 247's faces, holemap.py --model wempe at 8.89 and 8.57 px/mm; Kirov 009's and Poljot 20027's the same: sure), so 120°, 144° and 96° apart, where the drawings put 340, 100, 220; steel slotted heads Ø 6.1 ±0.2 × 2.0 (drawn 6.2) where the drawings' are brass 6.2 × 3.05. The ring's band and its tapped holes per version.
  • The bowl, re-measured: its outside with a pinhole camera fitted in the meridian plane, scaled by the rim's Ø 110.5, on Kirov 2973's bowl near side on (residuals under 0.3 px) and Kirov 247's: the thread r 55.25 down 5.55 from the rim's top, a collar r 56.6 to 7.76, the body r 52.4 (until then 51.8) to 46.7 (247: 47.0), a shallow cone to the foot r 36.7 at 55.3, the foot on to the drawn floor (its end isn't seen): likely. A cone that high leaves no room for the drawings' bore: the inside follows the outside, the bore r 49 then a cone 3.4 inside the outer one to the recess's wall (estimated; the movement's lowest parts clear it by 3.4 and more).
  • The brackets, the high form (Kirov 247's own bowl, 11_, 12_Kirow_247_E-Kontakt_*.jpg; Kirov 2973's the same; Kirow 422's too): each case bracket a flat plate 9.7 high (12.8 to 22.4 under the rim's top), its wings 27.5 either side of a block 8.7 wide which rises 1.8 over the rim's top, the pivot's hole 4.8 under its top (3.0 under the rim's top: ±2), the wings' slotted screws 16.8 from the block at 17.4 under, through the bowl's wall (the small holes in the bore of Kirov 247's and Kirov-Poljot 24020's bowls 16-21 under the rim are their ends: likely); the locking bracket an upright 11.7 wide, two screws in a vertical slot at 20.0 and 27.4 under, cranked out past the bezel to an L hook 3.8 over the rim's top, the pad the transit lock stops against (Romanov p. 204). So the 6MX's bowl, with its bezel, closing plate and movement, hangs 13.2 lower in the gimbals than the drawings' (case.js's bowlS, DY6; app.js adds the movement to it); the later Kirov-Poljot 24020's pivots stand 10.8 under the rim, as the drawings' nearly do.
  • The closing plate: a flat disc, no boss (Kirov 14917's foot square on, rAw2zmulpk8 0:11.75; Kirow 422's; a modern one, moMvyx8eXfo 7:20: likely), its screw's head about Ø 8 on its face, the domed knob about Ø 6.5 at r 19 ±2 (the drawings' 25); its groove, holes and spring as the drawings' (the spring unseen on any 6MX: Estimated), the spring's end shortened into the thinner plate.
  • The outer box: its front about 233 wide (±7 %, the inner box's 190 scaled on 13_Kirow_247_Kasten_1.jpg and Poljot 08479's), the notch a circular segment, chord 102, depth 33 (until then a half-round r 48), the catch 51 under the parting line. The lid's tab reads larger than the notch (chord 105-111, 41-44 high) and may lap over the body's front: drawn filling it (Unresolved). The parting line's height and the straps' places are hidden by the bag (estimated as before).
  • The seconds wheel: the gilt collet on its arbor under the wheel (6_Kiro_247_S.jpg) is the contact wheel's (below). Pillar 39 reads Ø 8.0 ±0.5, the drawn 8.1; its radius stays 37.3 (Estimated).
  • The electrical contact (Kirov 247's: leben-des-6mx/10_-12_Kirow_247_E-Kontakt_*.jpg, 6_Kiro_247_S.jpg, 2_Kirow_247_A.jpg and 3_Kirow_247_uZ.jpg against Kirov 1564's without one; Kirov 009's, 2973's, Poljot 08479's and Kirov-Poljot 24020's of the same design; Romanov 1975, p. 105's parts 52-69 and Figs. 100-101, p. 209; the user's choice, 17 October 2026, to build it). On the pillar plate's inner face by pillar 39, from 176.5° to 236°, a gilt base 58 (2 thick, its outer edge an arc r 45.7 past the plate's rim, cut round pillar 39; its inner edge from Fig. 100: estimate) screwed to the plate by two M1.7 screws 56 (above); on it, on black fibre 68 (1.8) and insulated by bushes 67 (their black flanges Ø 4.6 under the heads), two gilt blocks, 52 (+, 177.6-201°) and 57 (−, 209-231°), each held by two steel cheese-head screws Ø 3.1 × 2.6 (182.9°/193.3° and 214.6°/226.0°, r 43: the two steel heads seen under the top plate's edge are 57's); a gilt knurled contact disc 55 (Ø 11.9 × 1.2, 48 teeth) upright in its radial plane at 207.7° on a bracket on block 57, turnable to renew the contact (the user instruction); the lever 60 pressed on a staff 69 (206.2°, r 31.8 on Fig. 100 mapped, ±1.5; taken r 31.0, so the spiral's measured Ø 8.9 clears the disc) jewelled at both ends, a hole jewel and an end jewel in a setting in the base and in an L-shaped gilt cock over it under a cap plate, its stone 61 (a corundum pallet with a bevelled end) on the contact wheel 10.0 from the seconds arbor, its other arm (15.1) carrying the brass contact screw 54 with a lock nut, tangential at r 45.5, its point on the disc's low face; a flat copper-coloured spiral 59 (7 turns, Ø 8.9) from the staff's collet to a stud 53 on block 52, both the lead and the lever's return. The contact wheel 62 on the seconds arbor under its wheel (Romanov: fixed to it), on a gilt collet Ø 2.0 rising 3.0 above it (3.1 and 3.55 until 18 October 2026): 60 ratchet teeth, tips Ø 20.4 (likely), roots 18.6 (estimate), 8 spokes, one tooth left out. In the bowl, two flat brass springs 66 on black insulation, each held by two screws 65 through the wall, three tines bearing on a block's outer end; outside, their slotted brass heads and a brass socket for each lead, + at 200.6° and − at 235.9°, on black fibre washers, all 27.5 under the pillar plate's inner face (12_Kirow_247_E-Kontakt_3.jpg, a camera fitted on the band; the springs on 11_ and Fig. 101: likely; their sizes estimated, ±15 %). The heights from Fig. 101 (9.68 px/mm, which gives the seconds wheel's height to 0.06 and the 19 between the plates) and the S views (10.5 and 21 px/mm). Five more jewels, as the TU's 20 against 15 without the contact (checks.py JEWELS). It works as Romanov (p. 209) and the user instruction describe it: the seconds arbor turns 3° a beat, half a tooth; on one beat the wheel's sloping flank lifts the stone (the lever turns about 4°) and the screw leaves the disc, on the next the tooth's radial face lets it fall and the spiral closes it: open half a second, closed half a second, and at the missing tooth closed a second and a half, at the minute (train.js update, R.c6; which half-second is open isn't given: estimated). The parts the photographs show are where they show them; the stone and the staff's place, seen on no photograph, are Romanov's figure put on them (estimate). Rebuilt to the photographs (18 October 2026), 10_Kirow_247_E-Kontakt_1.jpg through photocompare.py's m6_contact camera (0.6 mm at the block screws) and 14_E-Kontakt1.jpg (another 6MX of the same design, the m6_contact_front camera, about 1 mm): a millimetre scale stood at the staff, the seconds arbor and the screw's tip through the first gives the heights, and the two together give places across the view (they look along nearly the same line, 14° apart, so depth stays Fig. 100's). The cock's arm −12.9 to −14.2, 1.3 thick (−11 to −13.2 before), its leg run up to it; its cap plate three lobes, the two screws and the end jewel in a row 2.1 either side (along (−0.97, 0.24) as triangulated), the arm rounded r 1.6 past the far screw (a round plate with its screws 75° either side of the arm's axis before); the spiral at −11.7 to −12.3 just under the arm, its end run out over the stud and bent down onto its top beside the clamp screw (head Ø 2.2) (−8.5 to −9.1 before, from Fig. 101); the lever gilt (steel before), the contact screw Ø 1.0 threaded, at −5.85 (the photograph's −5.15 ±0.6 taken at the top of its range, to pass 0.1 over block 52's top), held in a gilt block under the lever's end with a brass lock nut 1.1 across; the disc's knurl square, its low face recessed Ø 6.0, 0.3 deep (estimated), a slotted steel axle screw (head Ø 2.6) in it, no raised boss. Left as drawn: the cock's leg renders about 2.5 further from the disc across the view than both photographs show it, within Fig. 100's ±2 but at its edge; moving it needs the arm's root and foot, whose depth no photograph fixes (Unresolved). The fine check required: the stone's end narrowed by its bevel (0.3 at its point), the stud's outer face at r 44.0, one block screw 0.15 off pillar 39 and the cock's screw and pins placed clear of its leg (each within its reading). The base overhangs the pillar plate's window for the intermediate wheel (0.23 over it), so in the Exploded view the 6MX's intermediate wheel leaves toward the dial after its bridge, as a watchmaker takes it out, the lever, spiral and cock lift clear of the contact wheel first, and its seconds wheel rises 30.6.
  • The page's physics (the user's choice, 17 October 2026): the 6MX runs its own escapement, WPHYS.rev('6mx') with its weighed bodies (WESC.SET6, checked by tools/wempe_6mx.js against wempe_inertia.py --rev 6mx), its swing table and its 35-day trial (WEDATA.rev6, wempe_essaydata.js, its children run as the 6MX: wempe_load.js's MC_WREV), in the Swing and isochronism and the Rate and trial panels and in the export to Blender. With the contact wheel weighed on its seconds arbor (the escape arbor's body 10.89 g·mm² against the drawings' 9.96), its swing is under the drawings' over the whole wind (190.2-200.2° against 191.0-200.5°: tools/wempe_6mx.json, its escape arbor 10.19 g·mm² since 29 October 2026, the shorter pinion; 190.1-200.1° against 191.9-202.0° when first worked out), its rate against 12 h theirs to 0.01 s a day; the mainspring is the drawings' (the 1958 Navy repair book's 1.01-1.08 N·m fully wound is the first generation's MX, which a strip about 0.42 thick would give, but no 1950s source gives the 6MX's strip: Unresolved).
  • The contact revised (24 October 2026). The lever's boss sits on the staff just under the spiral's collet (−10.2 to −11.5), not at the screw's height: on Kirov 2973 (14_E-Kontakt1.jpg) and Kirov-Poljot 24020 (12_KirPol_24020_E-Kontakt2.jpg, 16.7 px/mm by the cock's arm) the boss is 0.1-0.3 under the collet, the staff bare steel under it, and the arm runs down from it to the screw's holder on block 52 (likely; Kirov 247's own lever is hidden behind the stud and holder). Both arms are drawn sloping from the boss to their ends at the old heights (−6.1 to −7.4); the stone arm's slope is estimated, since no photograph shows it. The staff is Ø 0.6 under the boss (8-11 px against the block screws' Ø 3.1 at 23-26 px/mm, a little further off: Ø 0.4-0.6) and Ø 1.0 above it. Until then the boss and both arms were flat at −6.1 to −7.4, 4.5 under the spiral, on a staff Ø 1.0 the whole way. The cock (its foot, leg, arm, cap plate and screws) was compared again on 2973's, 24020's and 247's photographs and left as it is. The block's stud has a real slot, 0.5 wide and 0.9 deep, square across the base (the loose block, 8_Gangfeder_mit_Kloben_Rus_einfach.jpg, 30.3 px/mm: 15-17 px across, running about 12 px down the stud's side; likely), in place of the kit's 0.35 × 0.55 at an arbitrary heading. The 6MX's block has no Ø 1.3 hole between its near steady pin and the stud (25 October 2026, the owner's choice): 05 04 01-4 drills one there from the plate's face to the detent foot's M1, and the German block in 10_Vergleich_CWW-6MX_Gangfeder_mit_Kloben.jpg shows it, but the 6MX's face is plain there on that photograph and on 8_Gangfeder_mit_Kloben_Rus_einfach.jpg (at about 30 px/mm it would be 40 px across: sure). The drawn versions keep it. The 6MX face's dot between the stud and the far pin (about Ø 0.3, a small hole or a punch mark) isn't drawn. The whole contact (on the pillar plate, on the seconds arbor and in the bowl) is hidden on the page unless Variants' Electrical contact is set to Shown (contact=1 in the link; the owner's choice, 24 October 2026); under ?qa it is shown, so every tool weighs and checks it as before, and the physics is the same either way.

Checked again against the photographs (29 October 2026). The 6MX's escapement, its block and the parts at their heights, each read on the photographs before the model's figures were looked at (Kirov 247's 8_Kirow_247_F.jpg at 18.3 px/mm, scaled by the escape wheel's tips, 257.5 px for Ø 14, and its pinion's Ø 2.97, 54 px; Kirov-Poljot 24020's 9_KirPol_24020_Feder2.jpg at 26.6): WEMPE-VARIANT-ESCAPEMENT.md at the root has every reading. Changed:

  • The upright is slit along the banking screw, parallel to the plate, from its end into the screw's hole: a line about 0.1 wide on both chronometers, the thread showing in it, 2.85-2.9 from the end face on 247 and 2.8 on 24020 (sure). The loose block's face toward the plate is plain (X5), which a slit parallel to the plate doesn't contradict: it doesn't show from that side. Built 0.12 wide, ending in the hole (its far edge 3.07 from the end), the upright's end extruded across with the slit and hole in its profile, as the 1943 block's.
  • The banking screw's head Ø 3.4: 3.45 ±0.1 on 247 and 3.43 on 24020 at the wheel's own scale (likely); the 3.2 came from scaling by the upright's 3.
  • The escape pinion 3.77 long, from 11.15 to 14.92 under the escape wheel, its foot about 2.2 over the pillar plate (likely ±0.1): the 3.9 and 1.5 read on the same photograph came from a tip span of 247 px (17.65 px/mm), where the tips measure 257.5.
  • The collet's end Ø 1.55: 1.37-1.57 on 247 at 6×, 24020's 1.58 (likely).

Matched: the base's 6.5 at its end, the stop screw's head (Ø 4.4 ±0.15, the model's 4.2) and place, the collet's length (5.19 ±0.1) and its diameter at the wheel, the wheel's rim 1.37. Not settled by any photograph: the adjusting slide and stud, the lower cock's plan and step (Unresolved), the upright's height (3.45 ±0.3 read against 3.0: possible) and the screw's axis 0.4-0.6 under its middle (one view: possible).

The sheet, Soviet 6MX against the drawings (18 October 2026). The panel's section after Variants lists every difference the 6MX version builds (app.js's X6: 22, grouped as frame, escapement, barrel, electrical contact, ring and dial, case and boxes), each with what the drawings have, what the 6MX has and how sure the reading is, as this section gives them. Choosing one turns the model to the 6MX and closes in on it, the rest see-through (VIEWER.focusOn, shared/viewer.js: the parts' box, or a place where a part's own box would lose the change, as for pillar 39, the hand-setting holes, hole 53 and the moved ring and dial screws); Drawings and Soviet 6MX flip the version where the camera stands; a view chosen, Reset, Back or Whole model ends it.

The geometry checks in the 6MX

The browser checks of section 1, run with the page set to the 6MX: its own parts, its case and boxes, against the same expected contacts and leftovers.

Its physics against the drawings

Its jewels in chatons change the holes' tolerance, not the train's efficiency (oiled steel in ruby and in brass has the same friction in the model's sources); its escapement at the first-drawn heights, with the first-drawn balance staff and collar, changes the bodies only, weighed on the page's solids in that version.

The escapement of 1943 against the drawings

The page's fourth version stands its escapement as the German movements photographed with the 1943 detent block are made: the first-drawn balance, rollers and escape wheel at their heights, the 6MX's detent and the block with its banking screw (the model's README, "The escapement of 1943 as photographed"). Its plan is the drawings' (the banking screw sets the drawn depth of lock), so, as for the 6MX, only its bodies change: weighed on the page's solids in that version and run through makeEsc (wempe_1943.js), and through dynamics.js --model wempe in time on the same bodies (300 beats, no tooth lost; the swing 198.7° against makeEsc's 197.6°). The page itself runs the drawings' escapement in this version.

17. The builds: a Wempe to navigate by

What a maker would build to navigate by: about two miles of longitude a month, 8 s after 30 days at sea. As drawn, the balance swings 191-200° over the wind, under the sources' 225-270°; the depth of lock has a window of 15 µm, too fine to set and keep as the stone and the teeth wear; and set as the 6MX passports show adjusters set the masses, it carries 17 s after a month. Two builds answer it, and the maker chooses (the model's README, "The build"; each choice the user's, 19 October 2026):

  • Both: the gold spring thinned to 0.06 over its first 3 mm from its bending point (Belyakov 1957: Lange's MX 0.06 at its bend; 05 04 01-2's 0.15 taken as the blank), which opens the lock's window to about 0.2 mm; the preload 0.8 g; endshake to the Soviet Navy's 1958 MX repair book; the temperature masses set to ±0.1° on more rounds of the trial.
  • The 1940s build: the drawings' drive and their carbon-steel mainspring, 0.37. A stronger carbon strip is past steel's limit.
  • The 1950s build: 1.26 times the drive (the repair book's mainspring torque), from a Nivaflex 45/5 strip 0.393 × 15 × 1,240 mm, its free curve set ×0.8 (Straumann's alloy, patented 1948: not in the Einheits-Chronometer's own decade; 0.377 at set ×0.6 until 19 October 2026, whose inner coils section 13's 3D analysis found at 3.25 GPa, past the alloy's 3.0: the thicker strip's are 2.88-2.96), its drive taken turn by turn through the drawn fusee (stronger fully wound, weaker run down); the maintaining spring banked while running, as the Hamilton's is.
  • Winding, both builds: the key let back at the end of each stroke, never let go outright (section 13: let go, the blow dents the click and the click wheel's tooth and bends the maintaining ratchet's brass teeth; no fix a maker could make keeps every part within its material).

The drawn versions' cross-checks between makeEsc, dynamics.js and the tripping frame are calibrated on the drawn detent; on the thinned gold spring three of them part on detail of the detent's motion (none bears on its safety), so each build is judged on what decides whether a made one works (wempe_build.js).

Made to the tolerances, and after the bench

Each build's tolerances, bench and Monte Carlo, run as section 12's with the build loaded (MC_WREV=build40, build): 2,000 movements each.

18. The mechanisms in turn: wear, the key, the motion work, the estimates

The Hamilton's model was checked mechanism by mechanism, as a maker would take its parts, by five tools beside the escapement's and the train's (its build report's section 11): wear, the key forced, the motion work, the train on sprung meshes and the estimates swept. The Wempe's counterparts follow, each reading the Wempe's own data (wempe_strength.js's loads, gearing_wempe.json's windows, tolerances_wempe.json's lock window, mechanisms_wempe.json, wempe_inertia.json) and its sheets. The train on sprung meshes (the Hamilton's traindyn.js) has no counterpart here: section 13's wempe_transmission.js already runs every mesh tooth by tooth through the beat (the meshes' forces, which rattle, the seconds hand's bounce) and weighs every body on the solids (its section 1; the escape wheel's inertia against WESC.SET's is invariants.py --model wempe's), so it is cited, not repeated.

Wear: how long each contact keeps its figure

Archard's law at every sliding contact (V = k F s / H; k from Rabinowicz, 1e-7 well oiled, 1e-6 poorly, 1e-5 once the oil has gone; the escapement runs dry, as a chronometer's does, at Rabinowicz's unlubricated non-metal on metal, 1.5e-6), the loads wempe_strength.js's fully wound, each depth against the tolerance it eats. An escape tooth's tip (gilt brass) wears as a wedge whose flat widens. The line is a service interval: the 1954 Soviet instruction's cleaning and fresh oil every three years (6MX-figures.md, п. 19); the TU's ten years' service life is reported against.

The key forced

A strong hand on the key's Ø 34.5 paddle (Imrhan and Munoz-Vasa's handles carried on past their 19 mm, an extrapolation; Swain's 1.06 N·m beside it), wound against the stop, and turned the wrong way. The 1943 key (51 00 11) is a one-way clutch, its coil spring gripping the tube one way ("Linksaufzug b. Rechtsdrehung entspannt sich die Feder"); the 1940 key it replaced is one-way too, its click spring drawn round its pipe (05-01_6; read as a plain key until 28 October 2026). The table's wrong-way lines are what a key that grips both ways would do.

The motion work and the up-and-down work, made on a CNC

Each mesh tooth by tooth on dial.js's tables, its depthing window (closer until its tips reach the roots, wider until it loses contact or its hand has a quarter of an hour of play) and the hole its stud must be bored to (gearing.js's rule, the window's close side less the stud's shake, halved). The cannon pinion's friction window is wempe_transmission.js's (section 13), put as a weight hung on the minute hand.

The estimates swept, with the bench's correction

What wempe_tolerances.js (section 12) doesn't sweep: the balance's free run-down (TF) over 80-200 s with the strip the bench's run-down test chooses, the pivots' shake against each mesh's window, the hairspring's length read four ways off 05 03_7, and its outer terminal curve formed by hand; for the drawings as last revised and both builds.

19. Making it: the frame under load, the order it goes together, each part on the machine

Sections 7, 12 and 17 ask whether a Wempe made to the drawings would hold together, keep time and pass its bench. Three more checks ask whether it can be made and put together at all, each on the page's own solids: the parts that hold the pivots solved as elastic bodies under the mainspring's load, the movement taken apart and put back in the order a repairer's book gives, and every machined piece read against what a lathe, a mill and a drill can cut.

The frame under load

fea.py --model wempe (the Hamilton's fea.py, its parts, arbors and fixings in wempe/checks.py's FEA): each part that holds a pivot of the going train (the pillar plate, the top plate, the barrel bridge, the fusee bush and the intermediate bridge) cut into brass bricks (E 100 GPa, ν 0.34) from its solid, at two sizes, the coarser a check on the finer; loaded fully wound and run down with the chain's pull on the drums' common tangent (the spring's moment at 05 06_20's level, wempe_physics.js, on the barrel's pitch radius; the fusee's radius and the chain's height at that turn) and each mesh's tooth force with its pressure angle (gearing_wempe.json), shared between each arbor's two bearings by the lever rule; each part held at its screws, the top plate on the three pillars (Ø 8.1, 19 long, bending as beams), the pillar plate at its rim in the movement ring, the parts put together by superposition. What it leaves out: the arbors' own bending, the jewels' settings (taken as the brass round them), friction at the fixings, the cocks (they carry the balance, none of the train's load).

The order it goes together

The Einheits-Chronometer has no overhaul manual of its own in the set; the Soviet Navy's repair book of 1958 (Эксплуатация и ремонт измерителей времени, pp. 59-60, "Порядок разборки и сборки") gives the order for the MX, its copy on the same frame, step by step: the hands, the dial, the motion work and the up-and-down pinion from the dial side; then, dial down, the balance's cock and the balance, the detent's block, the barrel arbor's ratchet, the barrel bridge, the fusee arbor's cork washer, flange and washer, the top plate on its three screws, and the rest; and together the same backwards. assembly.py --model wempe rasters every part as assembled into columns 0.2 mm apart (exploded.py's and overhaul.py's method), freezes the movement in one state, and draws each step's parts straight off along the arbors, or along a path of straight legs where a part leaves sideways: a pair fails if one passes through the other, or is dragged the long way out of a fit it sits in. Where the model's parts can't follow the book, or a real movement takes a part off another way (unhooked, unwound, turned to a gap, slid sideways), the step says so.

Each part on the machine

dfm.py --model wempe reads every machined piece off its solid (screws, jewels, springs, the chain, the dial's enamel and the hands left out: bought, stamped, rolled or wound): its sections sampled between every two heights at which it has a flat face, on a grid 0.01-0.06 mm square as the piece's size allows. It reports, against stated limits: walls in plan under mm (fragile in brass; teeth left to the gear cutter), slots narrower than an end mill of radius mm (a smaller mill, a slitting saw or EDM), the inside corners that mill leaves rounded, round holes and their depth over diameter (over 10 peck drilling, over 20 a gun drill or EDM; under Ø 0.2 a micro drill), the thinnest floor along the arbors, what is cut from each face and whether the piece is round about one centre (turned) or nearly (turned, then cut), undercuts (material above and below a gap: a lathe's grooving tool, or a side cutter on a milled piece), the setups that follow, and any void sealed inside one piece (it fails: no tool reaches it).

Every piece

20. The build book: what each part is made of, and how

The page's Making it (the Hamilton's maker's sheets, in the Wempe's words): each part card has its maker's sheet, its lines of the parts list with the fit bom.py measured on the model, the material and treatment its own drawing gives (the title block's Werkstoff, the notes' hardening and tempering, the surface marks, read off References/wempe/transcriptions/), and how it is made; its drawing to scale, drawn from the model's solids; and the whole build book to print, ending with the bench's tests for the 1950s build (section 17). Nothing is filled from practice: a part whose sheet leaves the Werkstoff blank, or which has no sheet in the set (the Wempe-Norm screws and pins, the parts drawn only on an assembly), says so. tools/wempe_makers.py writes the data (wempe/js/makers.js; --check in ci.py), book.py --model wempe checks the book as paper (every shown line on a sheet, each with a material or the reason it has none and a fit, every drawing at its stated scale and legible on A4).

226 lines as last revised (13 assemblies): 60 parts with their material on their own drawing, 153 without (54 Wempe-Norm parts whose standard sheets aren't in the set; the rest drawn only on an assembly, or with the Werkstoff left blank). 164 carry a fit measured on the model.
