The 1950s build's deviations on the cards

  • The gold spring thinned at its bend (both builds, the 1940s and the 1950s): „Goldblech 333 federhart“ (gold sheet 333 fine, spring-hard), as drawn; the blank 0.15 (05 04 01-2) thinned to 0.06 over its first 3 mm from its bending point, stoned or rolled; the rest as drawn. 05 04 01-2's 0.15 taken as the blank: Belyakov (1957, Table 3) gives Lange's MX 0.06 at its bend. Stiff, sprung back onto the horn after the discharge stone passes on the return, it sets the held tooth's stone ringing 113-116 µm; thinned it rings 44 µm and the lock's window opens from 15 µm to about 200 (0.102-0.280 mm at the 1950s build's drive: tools/wempe_detent_study.js, wempe_build.js).
  • Mainspring in Nivaflex 45/5 (the 1950s build (Straumann's Nivaflex: patented 1948); the 1940s build keeps the drawn carbon-steel strip): Nivaflex 45/5 (Co 45, Ni 21, Cr 18, Fe 5, W 4, Mo 4, Ti 1, Be 0.2 %); cold-drawn strip 0.393 × 15 × 1240 mm, its free curve set ×0.8, aged to over 3000 N/mm²; coiled; greased. 1.26 times the drawings' drive (the Soviet Navy's 1958 MX repair book's mainspring, 1.01-1.08 N·m fully wound, against the model's 0.83), which no carbon strip gives within steel's stress: the swing at 12 h 231.3° against the 1940s build's 202.9°, its inner coils 2.88-2.96 GPa fully wound on Nivaflex's 3.0, 30 days at sea 6.1 s. From 1.07 times the drive the maintaining spring closes onto its banking while running, as the Hamilton's does by design (13 min on it while the key turns).

The book's last chapter: the bench's 14 tests (tools/wempe_bench.js, the 1950s build), each on its part's sheet too. Not in the book yet: an order of assembly (the Hamilton's is its manual's Sec. VIII reassembly; no Wempe or 6MX assembly instructions are in the sources).

21. Navigating by it: the position a made Wempe gives at sea

Sections 11, 12 and 17 ask whether a Wempe passes its trial, can be made to its tolerances, and keeps about two miles a month in the builds. This section follows the whole chain a navigator depends on, from a chronometer as made to the ship's position. tools/wempe_navigation.js takes 2,000 made chronometers for each version, as wempe_montecarlo.js makes them after the bench. Their swing sets how much the oil's thickening moves the rate, and they are adjusted as each version is: as last revised, the masses within ±0.45° of their compensating place (the TU's trial, the 6MX passports' spread of C); the two builds within ±0.1° on further rounds of the trial. Each one is rated over ten days in port and carried sixty days to sea on wempe_errorbudget.js's voyage: a winter port (55 °F) into the tropics (85 °F) over the first twenty days, the scatter and drift calibrated on the 6MX's test cards, the barometer, the oil, and heavy weather one day in five. The navigator carries the rated rate, as rating.py's backtest does, so the error at sea is what the rate has wandered from it, added up.

Four seconds of time are a minute of longitude, which is one nautical mile at the equator and cos(latitude) miles elsewhere. The route is estimated, since no source gives one: from 45° N in port to 15° N by day 20, where the box reaches 85 °F. The fix itself has an error too. Bowditch gives a celestial fix by an experienced observer in favourable conditions a probable error of about ±2 miles (The American Practical Navigator, Pub. No. 9, 2019, Vol. 2, Ch. 3, "Navigational Errors"). It is taken here as a circular normal whose median radius is 2 miles (σ 1.70 a side, 95 % within 4.16), and the clock's error is added along the parallel. The criterion was stated before the results were known: after 30 days without a time signal, the chronometer should add no more than the sight itself. Its longitude error at the equator must be under 2 miles in the median (Bowditch's probable error, and the user's aim of about two miles a month) and under 4.16 miles in 19 voyages of 20 (the fix's own 95 % radius). Each figure is itself a sample of 2,000 voyages, so each is judged with its sampling error: 1,000 bootstrap resamples of the voyages (seeded, the same each run) give each figure's 95 % interval, and a half fails only if that whole interval lies over its limit. A figure over its limit whose interval still reaches it passes within sampling: 2,000 voyages can't tell it from one on the limit. One whose interval misses the limit by under 1 % of it is on the line, reported and not failed (the owner's choice, 26 October 2026, when the 1950s build's 95 % figure came to 4.34 miles with its interval from 4.160, against 4.158, once the error budget's calibration was made to stop wandering with its random draws: before, a run could land it either side). The limits were not moved. The 1950s build must not fail, and the tool fails if it does.

22. An independent pass: can it be built, and would it navigate?

The per-part audit of 25-26 October 2026 (six batches, WEMPE-PROVENANCE.md) changed parts the analyses above rest on: the escape pinion (4.0 long), the detent (its spring tapered, its heights), the endshake (0.06, the 1958 book's 0.05-0.07), the fusee body's place, the barrel's internals, the maintaining clicks and springs, the case and gimbals, and the mainspring's set (×0.75). This section is not a rerun. It reads each analysis again, adversarially, and asks three questions. Does it read the changed parts from their one source, or from a copy of their old numbers? Do its criteria match their sources? What does it assume that a maker couldn't meet? Two read-throughs were made, one hunting stale numbers and one weighing criteria and assumptions, and every finding was checked against the code before anything was changed.

Stale copies, found and fixed

  • The detent spring's thickness on the bench. Since 25 October the tripping frame takes the spring's thickness as a factor of the tapered spring's uniform equivalent, 0.0792 mm (1436's 0.09 at its ends and 0.07 at its middle). The bench's ring test (wempe_bench.js) still divided by 0.07, so every thickness in its table was a spring 13 % thicker than its label. Its band read 83-164 Hz; it is Hz, the spring as drawn ringing at Hz. The Monte Carlo (wempe_montecarlo.js) centred its detent springs on 0.07 against a band centred on 0.0792, and so replaced 4 springs in 2,000 movements that needed none (0 now). Both are fixed, and the bench, the Monte Carlo and the maker's sheets are rewritten for all three versions. No verdict changes.
  • The escape pinion's face in wempe_train.js was still 3 long (4.0 since the audit). Every mesh takes the narrower face, the wheel's rim, so no figure moves.
  • The damping measured on video (wempe_startup.json) had been fitted on 19 October, before batch 1 changed the balance's inertia and the detent's. Refitted on the escapement as it was that day, it gave TF 114.4 s (111-118); the model kept 111 s (the owner's choice, 26 October 2026), inside that range, and wempe_escapement.js checks that the model's TF lies inside the fit's range (it asked for within 2 s of its middle). The escapement's reconciliation and the detent's blade have since moved the fit to TF : the model keeps 111 s outside it (the owner's choice, 27 October 2026), and the check reports it.
  • Left as they are, no verdict moving: the frame's load takes the chain's radius fully wound as 9.355, the fusee's table at 8.75 turns, while the strength checks take its last entry, 9.30, a quarter turn past (0.5 %, the cautious side): both read the table, neither stale; wempe_wear.js takes the maintaining clicks' spring force as an estimated 0.44 N, and wempe_ratchets.js their springs' free span as 12-16, neither from the clicks as re-drawn in batch 5; the trial's label now reads "GOST 8916-58's class II trial, its limits GOST 8916-70's class 2" (6MX-figures.md).

Everything else reads its source: the energy budget's level (0.913) is computed live from the re-solved spring; the gimbals' bodies come from gimbals_wempe.json, reweighed after the threads (periods 0.67 and 0.77 s); the bench's endshake stacks agree with the escape arbor's and the fusee's drawn lengths; the chain's lever on the stop and in the strength checks is the fusee's own table's.

Both stricter readings are reported below; the verdict stays on this one (the owner's choice, 26 October 2026)

Can it be made and put together?

Yes, as drawn, with the work a 1950s shop would expect, and on nothing a maker can't do. Section 19's checks run on the page's own solids, which since 26 October carry their threads (ISO metric, the tapped holes threaded and each screw on its hole's helix). dfm.py finds no void sealed inside a piece. What it flags is ordinary watchmaking: walls under 0.15 mm (the escape wheel's and fusee's teeth and groove lands, the cannon pinion), two slots narrower than a 0.4 mm end mill (the upper cock's and the fusee's: a slitting saw), undercuts on eleven milled pieces (a side cutter) and the sharp inside corners an end mill leaves rounded. It also reads eight holes of Ø 0.077 in the fusee body, which no sheet has: a reading of the groove's surface, to be confirmed. assembly.py takes the movement apart and back in the 1958 book's order with nothing passing through anything. The fits the sheets left impossible were found and corrected by the audit itself (README, Readings corrected; the collet's bore against the 1946 staff, the hour wheel's collar against the dial). One fit a maker must make on the bench: the endshake. Made to the sheets' fits, every one of the Monte Carlo's 2,000 movements has some arbor outside the 1958 book's band (about five arbors each out of band, some of them binding), and the bench sets each.

Would it keep time to navigate by? The chain and its weakest link

The chain is the made chronometer's swing (wempe_montecarlo.js), its trial and voyage (wempe_errorbudget.js) and the position (wempe_navigation.js). What each source adds alone after 30 days at sea, median |error|:

As adjusted on the TU's trial, the masses set to the 6MX passports' ±0.45°, the temperature's residual dominates: the rate moves by up to 0.1 s a day for each °C, and the voyage climbs 16.7 °C in its first twenty days. With the masses set to ±0.1° (two or three more rounds of the 4 °C and 36 °C periods, about two weeks on the bench), drift becomes the largest term. That is a slow change of rate, calibrated on eight test cards as a constant slope, which a ten-day rating in port cannot see.

Why the drawn version fails. It is mostly not the low swing. It is the masses' setting: run the drawn escapement with the builds' ±0.1°, and it carries . The swing (193°, from the drive and damping the owner chose) is left only the difference between that and the builds' figures. Where the swing does matter is over a year rather than a month: at 193° the rate is about seven times as sensitive to the drive as the 1950s build's at 230°, so as the oil thickens between services it wanders more, and each voyage's fresh rating has more to take out.

What a maker must do on the bench

Pass the TU's trial; then keep repeating its 4 °C and 36 °C periods, five counted days each, moving all four masses by C/0.228 degrees each round (a pair alike, to keep the poise), until |C| is under 0.023 s a day per °C. That step decides whether a made one navigates. Then set every arbor's endshake to the 1958 book's band, the banking to the middle of the lock's window and the preload to its aim with wire riders, replace a detent spring that rings outside its band, change the strip if the mainspring's pull is out of its band, and turn the set-up until the swing stays in band over the whole wind (section 17's tests).

What the model assumes the maker achieves, and doesn't model. The ±0.1° assumes that a compensation, once set, holds: that moving the masses and tightening them again doesn't shift the poise, and that the nickel-steel rim doesn't age between the trial and the voyage. The scatter is white noise, and the drift a constant slope. The oil loses 0-10 % of the drive a year, linearly, its viscosity's change with temperature left out (it matters most to the drawn version). Missed or irregular winding is not modelled.

The verdict, version by version

    23. What stays open

    What the sources haven't settled, as the model's README lists it ( questions), each with the reading the model takes and what would settle it:

    • dialsvg.py --verify on Kirov 247's red serial (28 October 2026, the second drawing check's 7-M9): it exits 1 on the 6MX's dial, the red serial 10.62 mm² in the SVG against 10.54 on the page's canvas, 0.75 % against its 0.5 % limit; every shape agrees (0 px differing 3 px across) and the black ink of all three dials is 0.10-0.13 % over in the SVG. The excess is the same rasterising edge bias in all of them (the SVG's fill a fraction of a pixel wider along every edge), which on the serial's thin strokes, with several times the black ink's edge for its area, is a larger share: not a fault of the traced serial (dialface_kirov.js), whose outline is the photograph's. Left as it is: an area limit that knows the shape's edge length (or an absolute floor for so small an area) is the tool's to settle; ci.py runs only the stale check, which passes.
    • The escapement's dry tip wear short of a service interval (28 October 2026; the owner's choice: reported soft, ~~). With the gold spring's bending point at 05 04_1's drawn mark (6.15 from the stone, the second drawing check's 2-M3: sure; 6.7 before), the strip is stiffer and the lock's window narrows to 231.7-237.2 µm (237.9 before): wempe_wear.js finds the escape tooth's tip, run dry, wearing through the lock's room in about 2.8 years against the 1954 instruction's three-year interval (about 3 before). Oiled, every contact lasts far longer. To settle: whether the drawings allow a wider window (the drawn depth of lock, the preload, the builds' thinned gold spring).
    • The band's drum hook in the barrel (28 October 2026, the second drawing check's N-2; not in ci.py, which runs fine.py with the chain): fine.py --eval "document.querySelector('#conn button[data-v=band]').click()" finds the drum hook (05 07 03-3) 0.037 mm³ into the drum (batch 4's). The band's round hook in the fusee's flange, 0.550 mm³ until then, is gone: the fusee's cutter pocket is cut 0.2 deeper at the pin (the owner's choice, O-5; fusee.js).
    • makeEsc's work stepped by its own ride steps (27 October 2026, the owner's request to improve the isochronism; tools/wempe_cliff.js): the 0.29 s a day dynamics.js's cross-check found over the wind was makeEsc's, not the chronometer's. Its ride through the impulse timed each landing of the stone on the escaping tooth's back at the end of a quarter table step, which stepped the work 1-3 % about a degree apart and held the full-wind swing at 200.9° where dynamics.js runs at 204°; refined to 32-128 steps it converges on 203.9°. Each landing is now timed inside its step, the ride stepped eight times a table step (RSR) and the swing solved on the work averaged over ±0.5° (SMW): half the 0.98° the impulse raises the swing within each beat, since a real dip half a degree wide (201.5-202° at full wind) remains, which the balance crosses every beat. The swing over the wind is now 192.5-203.9° (197.4° at 12 h), the escapement's change over it +0.93 s a day against dynamics.js's +0.84 (−0.08 apart, the check back to 0.2), and with the drawn hairspring (HS −0.485) the chronometer's rate over the wind −0.14 to +0.24 s a day. What remains is the chronometer's own: the escapement gains about 0.8 s a day for each 10° and the drawn spring loses 0.49. Averaging changed nothing at 4 steps (the steps there are deeper than the window). The page reads the swing off WBANK.amp (tools/wempe_banking.js), a solve taking about a second.
    • The let-off in heat (27 October 2026; tools/wempe_thermal_frame.js, the report's section 9, "The frame, train and escapement in heat and cold"). Over the TU's 4-36 °C the train's depths, the endshakes, the depth of lock and the chain move under 4 µm, but the steel detent grows less than the brass frame that holds its foot, so the gold spring's tip draws 1.8-2.3 µm away from the staff at 36 °C (the published constants' middle and the corner that moves it most), taking 0.3-0.45° of the drawn 1.50° let-off. At about 1.0-1.1° the escapement loses its impulse (the tooth runs a pitch before it lands on the impulse stone: makeEsc, and dynamics.js --model wempe in time on the same settings, the swing 91-97°): the same edge that tops wempe_tolerances.js's lock window (its deepest lock lets off at 1.12°). The drawn lock (235 µm) holds at the constants' middle and not at the corner; the bench's (the window's middle, 238 µm) fails at 36 °C at both. The window that holds over 4-36 °C is 231.7-237.9 µm at the middle (6.2 µm wide against 12.7 at 20 °C), none at the corner. The owner's choice (27 October 2026): the window over 4-36 °C is the window. wempe_tolerances.js caps its top at the deepest lock set at 20 °C that keeps the swing in the guard band at the wind's lowest at 36 °C (wempe_escheat.js, the constants' middle): 231.7-237.9 µm (237.9 against 244.4 at 20 °C alone). The bench aims just under its top, 237.8 (the owner's second choice that day): a worn tooth's tip only makes the lock shallower, away from the let-off's cliff, and the dry escapement's tip wear (wempe_wear.js, about 2.1 µm a year) wants about 6.2 µm over the floor for the 1954 instruction's three years between overhauls, which the window's middle (234.9, 3.2 µm) gave for only 1.6; set there, a chronometer at the constants' middle has no heat margin at 36 °C until the teeth wear; the 1950s and 1940s builds' windows lose about 5 µm at the top (84-275 and 90-273 µm). Every version still works after the bench in the Monte Carlo (100 %). Still open: at the constants' corner no lock holds at 36 °C; more let-off (the discharge stone's reach or the gold spring's tip, both estimated where the sheets don't size them) would widen it. The escapement's and drive's share of the rate is small (C +0.008 s a day a °C, S +0.09 s at the middle).
    • The stone's blow on the escaping tooth's back, on a cliff (26 October 2026; the owner's choice: recorded, the transmission check's bracket reported). With the escape wheel as drawn (its web 0.7: the arbor 8.28 g·mm², JW 9.53), the locking stone, flung off the discharge stone and falling back, catches the escaping tooth's back 0.6 µm above its banking just before the back's end passes (13.47° of the balance, the back running away at about 0.29 m/s); its plastic landing pushes the wheel and gives the balance 0.0024 k a beat, 3.4 % of the impulse, 2.4° of swing. Whether it lands at all turns on a microsecond: with 0.25 g·mm² more at the escape wheel (8.82 and up) the tooth has passed first and the blow is gone. makeEsc counts it since then (RWD, Wempe only: the Hamilton's figures bit for bit), and agrees with dynamics.js within 1.2° and 0.3 s a day over 8.0-8.9; the meshed train in wempe_transmission.js lands as a rigid train of about 10.2, past the step, so its impulse work falls outside the two rigid trains it is bracketed by (reported, ~~). Until then makeEsc and the time model agreed only because at the old inertia (8.73) the blow had nearly vanished. The landing's plasticity and the back's end are estimates; a made Wempe's swing could sit either side of the step. Since 27 October 2026 (tools/wempe_cliff.js, which maps the work's steps about the swing at each drive and the beat's closure over the wind): with the blade centred the swing was held on that step at every drive (the step within 0.2-0.4° of the solved swing at 90-105 %, the beat closing 0.955-1.058 over the wind; wempe_escapement.js checks 12 h alone, 1.013), a stable pinning (under the step the blow adds work and the swing rises, over it the swing falls). With the blade built and the discharge stone's reach taking the gold spring's tip's slide about the offset flexure (Readings corrected) the step lies 3.5-5° under the swing at every drive from 85 to 105 % and the beat closes 0.97-1.01 over the wind (1.000 at 12 h); what is left is the stone's hops on the back through the impulse, a roughness of about 3 % (the swing at full wind held on one at 200.9°). The 6MX's heavier escape wheel (JW 10.45) puts its swing on such a hop's step at every drive (its beat 0.95-1.06; unchecked by the tools; clean with the blade centred).
    • Left open by the drawings check (26 October 2026, PLAN-wempe-drawing-check.md; each batch's report in drawing-check/, the ledger WEMPE-DRAWING-LEDGER.md). Corrected meanwhile are listed in RESOLVED.md; these are the readings no sheet settles, the sheets' own conflicts, and what the model can't yet build:
      • Kept, the sheets' own conflicts (27 October 2026, the open items settled): the set-up click's 17,4 overall against 17.53 from its 9,7, 7,5, r 1 and the base line (05 08 05-2: the figures drawn); the stop work's C-D (05 06_4) read from the hub Ø 21, its "1,76" 0.1 and "3,2" 0.16 off the bar the 22,5 and the "2" fix (the drawn bar kept; Estimated); the block screw on the plate table's hole 13 (23.41, Wempe 3955 23.36) against 05 04_1's 23,8; the Lange dial's own disc (1453/A) not built, the variant the printing only; the stud's round point and pin hole (the blank's, drilled at assembly); the bowl's tapped holes for the brackets' screws (embed). Each sheet's reading in the ledger WEMPE-DRAWING-LEDGER.md.
      • Readings not settled: the lid plan's Ø 6.4 circle (05 07 01-2).
      • Built short of the sheet, the tools' limits: the 1943 barrel arbor's hook hole right through its core (05 07 02; drawn 6 deep, as the 1941 one: a hole through a turned core's axis comes out of bore() open); the radial seat for the masses' screws WN-12 (their heads' faces follow the mass's round side instead); the blind pin holes' drill-point ends in the cocks and bridges (solidGeo can't close a blind cone from that side); the upper cock's setting screws' holes plain where they pass through the boss (they leave through its side); the first-drawn block (05 04_1's) not built apart; seams where fused pieces meet face to face (the fusee bush, the ratchet's cup, the detent's pieces).
    • The rigid train against the train on its meshes (19 October 2026, the physics pass; traced 25 October 2026): wempe_transmission.js, the whole transmission as bodies on its meshes, gives an impulse 5.1 % more work than the rigid train makeEsc, dynamics.js and the page take (3.8 % before the per-part audit's first batch reweighed the bodies; 2.1 % with the lock at 0.175, the preload 0.63 g and TF 108 s); as a drive it keeps the swing 6.2° higher than the rigid train's at 12 h. The cause is the train's backlash, not its meshes' give: stiffer meshes don't close the gap (×100 at a quarter of dynamics.js's step, which stiff meshes need: +4.5 %; ×0.5 +6.2 %; as drawn +5.1 % at either step), while the last mesh, the seconds wheel on the escape pinion, lets go about 1 % of the time: the escape wheel lands dead on its stone, the seconds wheel runs on into the backlash (170 µm), and at the release the escape wheel starts free of the train behind it. The tool now runs both rigid bounds, the whole train's inertia at the escape wheel (10.01 g·mm², makeEsc's JW 9.98) and the escape arbor's alone (8.73): 11.655 and 13.560 µJ, the meshes' 12.254 between them, 31.5 % of the way (a check), as a rigid train of about 9.68 g·mm² (9.61 interpolated linearly; a rigid twin at 9.61 comes within 1.1 %). Left for the owner's choice: makeEsc's Wempe JW at that equivalent inertia would raise the model's swing by about 6° (escgolden.js untouched: a Wempe setting); the drawn backlash is the teeth's own, so the meshed train is the better model of it. The check stays at 8° and 0.5 s a day until then. 28 October 2026: with the escape wheel's speed in the coupling dynamics.js's own (Physics: the transmission), the figures above no longer hold: the two rigid bounds give 13.713 µJ (the whole train, 9.56 g·mm²) and 14.430 (the escape arbor, 8.28), the meshed train 13.341, outside them on the low side (−52 % of the way, reported), as a drive −3.74° of swing on the mean of the 8 starts. The differenced speed's false kick at each impact had been adding about 2.4 % to the meshed train's work; what the backlash's equivalent inertia is, now that the meshed train sits below both bounds, is open.

They look added on that chronometer (a pin spanner's, perhaps: moderately sure). The 6MX has no such plate (a sliding shutter; Kirow 422's bottom, 11_Kirow_DEC_422_Gehäuse.jpg, a flat disc); GUB 11307's (Rwr93vdA8cw 9:34, 9:48, about 9 px/mm) has a plain boss face round its screw, as the sheet's blind hole would leave it. It lies under the sources' band, 225-270° (the 1954 Soviet instruction, for chronometers in general), by 25.5-36.5° (23-33° before the physics pass; the train on its meshes would take about 4.6° of it back: above): with the damping now measured on a running 6MX (102-125 s at the model's swing, the model set to it), the drive's level is the likelier cause (05 06_20's measured pull is 0.80 of the solved 0.37 strip's: Physics, energy). tools/wempe_escapement.js reports it (~~); its own 180-270° check is only a guard against the model's swing falling. A 6MX on video swings 110-185° part wound, out of its bowl (References/wempe/VIDEOS.md, "Measured"): its damping bears out the model's TF, its swing says nothing of a wound Wempe's. But Belyakov's radii don't close with the centre distance for either chronometer as the models build it (the Wempe's wheel r 7 and impulse circle r 3.8 less the teeth's 0.39 into it make 10.41 against 05 04_1's 10.00; the Hamilton's Table 1, 6.575 + 3.70 − 0.3 = 9.98 against 9.40), so his linear figures may be measured another way (his "lock δ 1°" at the detent's locking arm, 14.25, is an arc of 0.25): settle how before using them.

The sheet's 0.15 may be the blank, thinned at the bend as a passing spring usually is: the most consequential of these.

No photograph shows the dial side in profile.
    • The balance holding device (05 36), not built (the user's decision, 18 October 2026). How it works is Wempe's patent DE 742 143 (John Schwarzer, filed 26 November 1941, References/wempe/documents/, figs. 1-4): two brass tongs (36 00 01-1, every figure) on one screw at hole 51 in the top plate's pocket, pressed shut by a leaf spring round them (the dark band 05 36's plan draws round their backs and bosses), close concentrically on a brake ring on the staff ("Bremsring aus Preßstoff", moulded phenolic: 05 36's Schnitt A-B draws it cross-hatched under the collar's flange, Ø 6.1 scaled, bore 2.6, its foot 0.2 under the plate's inner face; the plan's dotted ring Ø 5.85), so the balance stops without side load on its pivots; a bell crank (27, U 02) under the plate on a screw at 52, held by a coil spring to a pin at 53 against the flattened eccentric end of a knob's shaft in the case (28, U 03; the knob 1, turned 180° between "frei" and "fest", held by a spring and a detent pin), carries an upright pin in the tongs' notch, which spreads them open at "frei". Built in the version as first drawn on 18 October 2026 and taken out again the same day: drawn open, the tongs clear the impulse roller (the pocket, tapered 10 to 8 wide since 15 October 2026, lets each turn 3.8°, where the 8-wide pocket read until then allowed 0.8°), but the lever, traced on 05 36's plan put on holes 23, 51 and 52 (12.31 px/mm, 0.06 mm), runs 0.9 deep through the 1941 escape wheel (its teeth 0.5-1.9 under the plate, the lever 1.35 thick just under it: fine.py, 2.4 mm³) and grazes the 1941 detent (0.1), as it runs through the detent block of 05 04 01-4 (8.7.43) as last revised; and the 1946 hub has no ring where the tongs close (its neck Ø 2.63). 05 36 is drawn on the lever plate (its spring pin lands by the lever plate's hole 53, O 13.0, not the detent plate's, O 15.0) and 127-556 is the Luftwaffe's lever chronometer BC 1010 ("Unruh-Arretierung": Knirim; the hand setting, above): the device is that chronometer's, whose escapement (05 04_20, _21, 05 03_1) isn't built. No photograph shows one on a detent Wempe: Wempe 3955's plate has holes 51-53 empty (13_Wempe_3955_obere_Platte_unten.jpg), the 6MX uses transit dampers; Wempe 2965 (lever, "Anhaltevorrichtung") and 2900 (lever, "Arretierung des Werkes") were sold with one, not photographed in a way that shows it. The 1943 plate keeps the pocket and holes 51-53, so a detent chronometer may have had one, its form not in the set.
    • The case (P1f; the sources read again 16 October 2026, the 6MX gallery among them):
      • The bowl's "Gewicht 350 gr.": the casting as drawn is about 152 cm³ (05 01_2's section: the wall 4, the bottom 6.5), 1.34 kg in brass (gimbals_wempe.json); 350 g is 2.3 g/cm³, which no moulded case reaches (Buna or Bakelite 180-210 g, a mineral-filled phenolic about 300) and an aluminium casting only nearly (about 380 machined), and "Ms-Sandguß (Kokillenguß)" names a metal casting. Wempe 3955's Bakelite bowl (16_Wempe_3955_Gehäusetopf_Kardan.jpg) is beaded and rounded, not R-05 01 00-1's 40° cone: an undrawn bowl. The 6MX's TU gives the whole chronometer ≤ 2.2 kg (6MX-figures.md, TU 1.2.8), where the model's bowl and ring alone weigh 3.26 kg: if the TU's mass leaves out its box, the bowl would be about 280 g, near the sheet's 350 (moderately sure the brass bowl is too heavy; whether the TU's "масса" counts the box isn't said). The machined bowl's sheet (05 01 00-1 without the R-) would settle it.
      • The bezel: screwed onto the bowl (likely): Wempe 5377's bezel is knurled at its lower edge (bonhams_26816_327_wempe5377_type05.jpg, sure; its case later), Wempe 3955's edge serrated (moderately), Wempe 8711's "threaded glazed bezel" (Antiquorum's text, catalogue-de-en.md), and 05 01 01 draws a thread's zigzag hidden in the lower bore (about 3 teeth over 4.4: likely); the 6MX's bowls (KirPol 24020, leben-des-6mx/13_, 14_KirPol_24020_E-Kontakt*.jpg; Kirow 247 12_Kirow_247_E-Kontakt_3.jpg) have a thin threaded collar at the top, about 5 turns at about 1 pitch, the ring's flange on a step inside it. The thread isn't sized on any sheet: built since 24 October 2026 at the 6MX's size and pitch (the bowl's rim turned down to it: The bezel and glass).
      • The ring's pin: no notch (05 01 01 draws the bezel without one; a notch in the bezel at 12, estimated, was built until 21 October 2026). A screwed bezel can't hold a notch to the pin, and KirPol 24020's bowl has the notch cut down through its threaded collar at 12 o'clock, about 1.6 wide and 4-5 deep (sure for the 6MX); so the Wempe's is likelier in the bowl, but 05 01 01 lays the flange in the bezel's recess, above the bowl's top face, where only the bezel meets the pin. With the bezel built to 05 01 01, which also marks its lower bore threaded, the pin stands clear: its seat, likely in the machined bowl, isn't drawn.
      • The Feststeller: on Wempes 4585 (rmg_L5393_wempe_wartime_001.jpg) and 5377 a knurled knob about Ø 20-21 on a short post, on a flat lever on a block on the right wall, with an upright pin about Ø 4 on the lever between the knob and the ring, where Schnitt A-B draws a circle Ø 8.6 under the lever (built Ø 8, as the sheet); the knob's top about 10 (5377) and 17-19 (4585) over the lever against the model's 15.3 (rough readings in perspective; the "17" from the front wall agrees). A side-on photograph of a Wempe's lock with the ring in place would settle the heights. Wempe 3044 (milivault_529241_wempe3044_screen.png, from above, rough) has the pin's round head, Ø 8.7 ±1, slotted, built Ø 8.7 × 2.5 on the drawings' case (its height estimated; the 6MX's pin kept plain), its lock's bracket a black block about 20 wide (the model's seat 18, kept), and its lever about 45 long along the front wall against 05 01's 28 (kept: the sheet decides; it may be another lever).
      • The Zunge (P. 51 00 02-2): on Wempes 4585 (aluminium) and 5377 (brass) the box's latch is an angle plate at the front's middle on the body, its top flange slotted about 6.5 long, with a knob about Ø 7 beside the slot, and an angle plate on the lid with a C-shaped hook into that slot; the model's tongue swinging on the lid's front over a keeper doesn't match. The Zunge (iron 10 × 4, 45 long, the M3.5 for a knob, a thinned round end) fits as the bolt behind the body's plate, which the knob moves to catch the hook (inferred); how it moves isn't seen. The 6MX's boxes have escutcheon hasps instead.
      • The box's height (25 October 2026, decided, nothing changed): 05 01's note gives "Holzgehäuse 185 × 185 × 180 mm außen" (sure); 51 00 10 ("Änderung von 51 00 10", gez. 14.7.42) draws the side panel square, 185 wide (±0.5) and 185 high (both figured; the outline 436 × 437 px at 2.38 px/mm), with the pivot's M6 105 over its bottom and the parting line 11.5 over that, so the same box. 05 01 was drawn 30.10.40 and reissued unchanged as working copy 4 (28.6.46, stamped 31.3.47), so its 180 is both the earlier figure and the latest one issued; the handle's sheet is a change to the handle, its panel drawn round it. Kept 180 in every drawn version: the 185 would only make the lid 5 taller (68.5 over the parting line against 63.5), the parting line, the pivots and the gimbals where they are. A measured height of a 1940s Wempe box would settle it (Lange 5499's auction gives 183 × 172 × 180, another maker's box, its axes not named).
      • The pins over the outer pivots (25 October 2026; built, Estimated): 05 01's elevation alone draws them, without a number or part line, inside drawn in crossing coils (a thread or a spring); no photograph shows one (Greenwich's wartime Wempe's side walls' tops over the pivots plain at about 2.5 px/mm, Wempe 6161's box later, with a rebated lip). Whether they locate the lid, catch it (a ball catch) or are something else isn't settled; a photograph of a 1940s box's parting face, or the box's own sheet (127-556.02), would settle it.
      • The Holzkasten's own sheet (127-556.02) isn't in the set; 127-556.02 U 01 (05 01_6, parts -01 to -05) is the 1940 key; the 1943 key is 51 00 11 (05 01_7), its parts 51 00 11-1 to -6 and 05 01 02-2, -3; each fits the holder in the box (the second drawing check's 10-M13).
    • The escape wheel's web recess against its teeth's floor (25 October 2026, dfm.py; Making it): the recess Ø 11.62 (05 04_7.2 scales 11.65) lies 0.04 inside the 1942 tooth form's floor Ø 11.7, leaving a sliver of brass about 0.04 wide and 0.6 high in each gap, which no maker would leave; built as the sheets give it. A sheet giving the recess's diameter as a figure would settle it.

    What the tools flag

    Every ~~ the checks above print, together: what they report without failing on.

      Reproduce

      From marine-chronometer-source/wempe/verification/:

      node reportdata.js        # every Wempe check run (the full runs, at once), and the figures: assets/data.json (about 9 minutes)
python geometry.py        # the browser checks on the Wempe's page, one after another: assets/geometry.json (about 11 minutes; section 19's fea, assembly and dfm about 16 more, each also writing its own JSON in assets/)
python build_report.py    # this page, index.html (a second)

      Each tool can be run on its own from marine-chronometer-source/chronometer-working-model/tools/ (the commands are beside each tool's checks above). The model's ci.py runs the quick forms of all of them on every change, and the full runs with --full, but three: the readings off the videos (wempe_swing.py, acoustic.py --model wempe), which need the videos, and the start-up fit made on them (wempe_startup.js), whose result wempe_escapement.js checks the model's damping against. This page is rebuilt when their results change.

      Sources

      The model's sources, as its README gives them:

      • The works drawings, References/wempe/drawings/ (© Johannes Altmeppen, by courtesy of Gerhard D. Wempe KG, 2017), as transcribed in References/wempe/transcriptions/05-08-frame.md and checked on the sheets themselves, cropped and enlarged wherever a number mattered. The frame's sheets are 05 08_1a/1b (Oberplatte, 05 09 01), _2 (Oberplatte kompl., 05 08 01), _3a/3b (Unterplatte, 05 08 02-1), _32.2 (Unterplatte kompl., 05 08 02), _4 (Unruhkloben unten, 05 08 00-2), _5 and _6 (Unruhkloben oben, 05 08 03-1, and the kompl. 127-556.04 U30), _7 (Werkring, 05 08 00-3), _8 (Schneckenfutter, 05 08 01-2), _9 (Staubfutter, 05 08 01-3), _10 (Zwischenbrücke kompl., 05 08 04), _11 (Pfeiler, 05 08 00-1), _12 to _14 (Federhausbrücke kompl., 05 08 05; Federhausbrücke, 05 08 05-1; Sperrkegel, 05 08 05-2), and sheet 001 (the movement in plan at 2:1).
      • The coloured section (drawings/Wempe_Einheitschronometer.jpg): the whole movement in one unrolled section, with the parts' numbers, including the Wempe standard parts (WN) that have no sheet in the set. Measured on it where no sheet gives a size, scaled on the pillar's 8.1 and the 19 between the plates (28.3 px/mm in a 3× crop, the same both ways where it was checked).
      • Photographs of genuine German movements: Wempe 3955 above all (photos/dg-chrono-dec/): 2_Wempe_3955_A.jpg, the top plate square-on on millimetre paper (8.82 px/mm at the plate, from the pillar screws' 62.41 and 58.7 mm apart); 3_Wempe_3955_uZ.jpg, the dial side; 12_ and 13_Wempe_3955_obere_Platte_*.jpg, the top plate off, both faces; the side views 4-7_Wempe_3955_*.jpg. ALS 5177 and the Kirow movements likewise. The 6MX differs (see References/wempe/README.md) and isn't evidence for the frame.
      • The 6MX's test cards (photos/dg-chrono-6mx-gallery/bilder-zum-6mx/: eight passports and attestats of Soviet 6MXs, 1953-1993, transcribed in References/wempe/documents/6MX-figures.md, section 8): the scatter and drift and the masses' setting the trial is run with, and the check on its secondary error.
      • National Bureau of Standards, Circular 58, Invar and related nickel steels (2nd ed., 1923), Tables 5 (p. 86) and 13 (p. 90): Guillaume's nickel steels' expansion, a + 2bt, by their nickel; the rim's 42-44.4 % "anibal" quadratic −3.4 to −2.51 × 10⁻⁹ a °C² (tools/wempe_thermal.js).

      And for the methods:

      1. Хронометры морские 6МХ. Технические условия, TU 25-07.1533-84 (1st Moscow Watch Factory): the trial and its limits; Instruction 246-54 for checking standard chronometers (1954): the swing for chronometers in general, the banking, the start.
      2. V. A. Shpolyanskii and A. M. Kuritskii, Spuskovye regulyatory priborov vremeni (Moscow 1963): marine chronometers' balances, the 6MX's integral balance and banking screw.
      3. E. Phillips, "Mémoire sur le spiral réglant des chronomètres et des montres", Annales des Mines (1861): the terminal curves' conditions.
      4. S. Timoshenko, "Analysis of bi-metal thermostats", Journal of the Optical Society of America 11 (1925): the bimetal's curl.
      5. National Bureau of Standards, Circular 58, Invar and related nickel steels (2nd ed., 1923), Tables 5 and 13: the nickel steels' expansion by their nickel, the secondary error's quadratic.
      6. C.-E. Guillaume, Nobel lecture (1920), and VintageWatchstraps, "Temperature Compensation by Nickel Steels": the nickel steels and the integral balance's secondary error at the Neuchâtel trials.
      7. M. A. Crisfield, Non-linear Finite Element Analysis of Solids and Structures, vol. 1 (1991), ch. 7: the co-rotational beam element; J. S. Przemieniecki, Theory of Matrix Structural Analysis (1968): the frame element and its consistent mass; P. Wriggers, Computational Contact Mechanics (2006): penalty contact.
      8. NORDFORSK, Assessment of Ship Performance in a Seaway (1987): the operability limit; MARIN (IMDC 2024) and Jachowski et al., KONES (2012): merchant ships' roll periods.
      9. J. F. Archard, "Contact and rubbing of flat surfaces", Journal of Applied Physics 24 (1953); E. Rabinowicz, Friction and Wear of Materials (2nd ed., 1995): the wear law and its coefficients. A. Imrhan and C. Munoz-Vasa, Industrial and Systems Engineering Review 1(2) (2013), and Swain et al. (1970): a hand's torque on small handles. EN 10270-1: patented cold-drawn spring wire's strength.
      10. Mainspring friction and losses: ICMFF9 (gruppofrattura.it), "the torque during unwinding is 10 to 20 per cent less than that during winding"; lubricated steel on steel, the CRC Handbook as cited in US 3,939,081.
      11. The Hamilton's reports, whose tools these are: Would a chronometer made to the model run and keep time? and Does the model behave like a real Hamilton Model 21?
